<tbc>Deterministic Distance Selection in _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) Time

Haitao Wang<sup>∗</sup>

**Abstract**

Let _P_ be a set of _n_ points in the plane. Given an integer _K_ with \(1\le K\le\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{2}\), the distance selection problem asks for the _K_-th smallest distance among all pairwise distances of the points of _P_. The problem has been studied extensively over the past four decades. Recently, Chan and Zheng (2023) gave a randomized algorithm with _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) expected running time, while the best known deterministic algorithm runs in _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>log_n_) time. In this paper, we present a deterministic _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>)-time algorithm for the problem, matching the best known randomized complexity.

We also consider the more general bichromatic version of the problem, where two point sets _A_ and _B_ are given, with _m_=|_A_| and _n_=|_B_|, and the goal is to find the _K_-th smallest distance among the _mn_ distances between points of _A_ and points of _B_. For this problem, the best previously known algorithm runs in _O_((_m_log_n+n_log_m+m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>)log(_m+n_)) time. We present a new deterministic algorithm with running time _O(m_log<sup>2</sup>_n+n_log<sup>2</sup>_m+m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>).

_Keywords:_ Distance selection, geometric optimization, distance counting, hierarchical cuttings, biclique partitions, range searching

## 1 Introduction

Let _P_ be a set of _n_ points in the plane. Given an integer _K_ with \(1\le K\le\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{2}\), the _distance selection problem_ asks for the _K_-th smallest distance among all pairwise distances of the points of _P_.

Distance selection is a fundamental problem in computational geometry. Besides its intrinsic interest, it serves as a prototype for a broad class of geometric optimization problems whose optimal objective values are realized by interpoint distances [3, 5, 9, 18, 19, 27]. One may even regard it as a geometric analogue of the classical selection problem [7]. The problem can be solved trivially in _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) time. The first subquadratic algorithm was given by Chazelle [11]. Later, Agarwal, Aronov, Sharir, and Suri [2] obtained an _O(n_<sup>3/2</sup>log<sup>5/2</sup>_n_)-time algorithm, which was subsequently improved by Goodrich [17] to _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>log<sup>8/3</sup>_n_) time. Katz and Sharir [20] further improved the running time to _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>log<sup>2</sup>_n_). Wang and Zhao recently reduced it to _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>log_n_) in ESA 2023 [28].

All of the above algorithms are deterministic. Several randomized algorithms are also known. The randomized algorithm of Agarwal, Aronov, Sharir, and Suri [2] runs in _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>log<sup>8/3</sup>_n_) expected time. Matoušek [22] later improved the bound to _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>log<sup>2/3</sup>_n_) expected time. Most recently, Chan and Zheng [10] obtained a randomized algorithm of _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) expected time. Their algorithm uses random sampling and is reminiscent of the randomized linear-time selection algorithm of Floyd and Rivest [16]. The complexity can also be expressed as a function of _K_. In particular, combining Chan’s randomized optimization framework [8] with the result of Wang [24] yields an _O(n_log_n+n_<sup>2/3</sup>_K_<sup>1/3</sup>log<sup>5/3</sup>_n_)-time randomized algorithm, which is particularly attractive when _K_ is relatively small.

Like Hopcroft’s problem and several related geometric range searching problems [10, 15], it is possible that distance selection has complexity \(\Theta(n^{4/3})\), although no matching lower bound is currently known. In particular, many problems whose best known upper bounds are _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) admit \(\Omega(n^{4/3})\) lower bounds, at least in a restricted partition-based computational model [15], such as Hopcroft’s<tbc>

<sup>∗</sup>Kahlert School of Computing, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT 84112, USA. `haitao.wang@utah.edu`

problem \[10\], segment intersection counting \[10\], computing closest points for segments \[6, 25\], computing many faces in line arrangement \[1, 4, 13, 14, 23, 26\], etc. If a similar lower bound could be established for distance selection, then the randomized algorithm of Chan and Zheng \[10\] would be optimal. On the deterministic side, however, the best known complexity remained _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>log_n_) \[28\], leaving a logarithmic gap between deterministic and randomized algorithms.

### Our result.

In this paper, we close the gap between the best known deterministic and randomized complexities by presenting a deterministic _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>)-time algorithm for distance selection.

We consider a more general bichromatic version of the problem. Let _A_ and _B_ be two sets of points in the plane with _m_=|_A_| and _n_=|_B_|, respectively. Let _S_ denote the set of all pairwise distances between points of _A_ and points of _B_. Given an integer _K_ with \(1\le K\le mn\), the goal is to compute the _K_-th smallest distance in _S_. The original monochromatic problem can be easily reduced to this bichromatic problem.

We first consider the symmetric case _m=n_. Previous work typically solved the bichromatic problem first (with the same time complexities as discussed above), with the monochromatic problem obtained as a consequence. We follow the same approach. Our main result is a deterministic _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>)- time algorithm for the symmetric bichromatic distance selection problem.

We also study the asymmetric case \(m\neq n\). For this problem, the best previously known algorithm runs in _O_((_m_log_n+n_log_m+m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>)log(_m+n_)) time \[28\]. By extending the framework developed for the symmetric case, we obtain a deterministic algorithm with running time _O(m_log<sup>2</sup>_n+n_log<sup>2</sup>_m+m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>). Note that if _m=O_(1), then the running time becomes _O(n_), matching the complexity of the classical linear-time selection algorithm. On the other hand, if _m=n_, then the bound becomes _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>), matching the complexity of our symmetric case algorithm. Thus, the asymmetric bound naturally interpolates between linear time and the symmetric _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) time.

## 1.1 Our techniques

We give an overview of our algorithm on solving the symmetric case bichromatic problem.

Like the previous deterministic algorithms \[20, 28\], our algorithm follows a prune-and-search framework. Let \(\delta^*\) denote the sought _K_-th smallest distance in _S_. The algorithm maintains an interval _I_ containing \(\delta^*\). In each iteration, the goal is to shrink _I_ to a smaller interval \(I'\subseteq I\) such that \(\delta^*\in I'\) and \(|S\cap I'|\le\rho\cdot|S\cap I|\) for some constant \(\rho<1\). Repeating this process for _O_(log_n_) iterations reduces the number of candidate distances to a manageable size. To implement the framework efficiently, two bottlenecks must be overcome.

### Two bottlenecks.

The first is a _decision bottleneck_. Given a value \(\delta\), we need to determine whether \(\delta<\delta^*\). Observe that \(\delta<\delta^*\) if and only if \(K_\delta<K\), where \(K_\delta\) is the number of distances of _S_ at most \(\delta\). Hence, we need a _decision algorithm_ to compute \(K_\delta\).

The second is a _representation bottleneck_. Given an interval _I_, we need a compact representation of the distances in \(S\cap I\) so that we can select a small set of representative distances. These representative distances are then used to shrink _I_ to a smaller interval \(I'\). Conceptually, this step plays the role of a deterministic sampling procedure.

In the algorithm of Katz and Sharir \[20\], both bottlenecks were handled in _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>log_n_) time, leading to an overall running time of _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>log<sup>2</sup>_n_).

Wang and Zhao \[28\] improved the framework by using a recent counting algorithm of Wang \[24\], which computes \(K_\delta\) in _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) time for any given \(\delta\). This matches an \(\Omega(n^{4/3})\) lower bound in a restricted model \[10, 15\], and therefore essentially settles the decision bottleneck. To address the representation bottleneck, Wang and Zhao introduced a new partial biclique partition technique (called _partial batched range searching_ in \[28\]). Their technique produces a compact representation of most,<tbc>

but not all, distances in \(S\cap I\), while keeping the representation error sufficiently small for the prune- and-search framework to remain correct. As a result, each iteration runs in _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) time and the overall running time becomes _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>log_n_).

## Our solution to the bottlenecks.

To obtain an _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>)-time algorithm, we address the two bottlenecks in different ways.

For the decision bottleneck, the lower bound for exact counting essentially blocks any further improvement. Since a prune-and-search algorithm requires _O_(log_n_) iterations and each iteration appears to require at least one decision query, it is difficult to avoid the _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>log_n_) barrier using exact counting. In contrast, the randomized algorithm of Chan and Zheng \[10\] uses random sampling and therefore needs only _O_(1) counting queries, leading to an _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) expected-time algorithm.

The key observation behind our deterministic algorithm is that the prune-and-search framework does not require the exact number of distances in \([0,\delta]\). An approximation is sufficient, provided that the approximation error is carefully controlled. We prove a new _approximate counting theorem_ (Theorem 1) that computes an approximate count for \(K_\delta\) in _o(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) time. Moreover, the running time decreases as the allowed error increases. The theorem immediately yields a _quasi-decision_ procedure (Theorem 2), which replaces the exact decision algorithm of Wang \[24\], and the procedure runs in _o(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) time. This does not contradict the \(\Omega(n^2)\) lower bound for exact counting, because the quasi- decision procedure is allowed to return "unsure" when the threshold is too close to the true count.

For the representation bottleneck, we further enhance the partial biclique partition technique of Wang and Zhao \[28\] and make it significantly more efficient. Two new ingredients are introduced. First, we use the \(\Gamma\)-framework of Chan and Zheng \[10\] to accelerate point location operations once the subproblem sizes become sufficiently small. Second, we introduce a new notion called _capture cells_ in hierarchical cuttings. Capture cells allow us to represent only a carefully selected subset of the distances while still guaranteeing that a constant fraction of all relevant distances are recorded. The idea of using capture cells is crucial to the success of our approach and is one of the most interesting components of this paper. This leads to a new _distance representation theorem_ (Theorem 3) that runs in _o(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) time.

## Putting the pieces together.

For a positive integer _i_, let log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_ denote the _i_-fold iterated logarithm of _n_, i.e., log<sup>(1)</sup>_n_=log_n_, and log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_=log(log<sup>(_i_-1)</sup>_n_) for \(i\ge 2\).

Our algorithm proceeds in _O_(log<sup>∗</sup>_n_) phases and maintains an interval _I_ containing \(\delta^*\). For _i_=1,2_,...,O_(log<sup>∗</sup>_n_), the goal of the _i_-th phase is to transform an interval _I_ satisfying<tbc>

\(|S\cap I|=O\big(n^{4/3}(log^{(i-1)}n)^4\big)\)

<tbc>(and _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) when _i_=1) into a smaller interval \(I'\subseteq I\) satisfying

\(|S\cap I'|=O\big(n^{4/3}(log^{(i)}n)^4\big),\)

while maintaining \(\delta^*\in I'\). Initially _i_=1 and \(I=(0,+\infty)\), and hence \(|S\cap I|=O(n^2)\).

The _i_-th phase consists of _O_(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_) iterations. Each iteration, which reduces the remaining candidate distances by a constant fraction, takes _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_) time for _i_=1,2, and _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_)<sup>2</sup>) time for \(i\ge 3\). Consequently, the first two phases each require _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) time, while the total time of all remaining phases is

\(O\left(n^{4/3}\sum_{i=3}^{O(log^*n)}\frac{1}{log^{(i)}n}\right)=O(n^{4/3}).\)

After _O_(log<sup>∗</sup>_n_) phases, we obtain an interval _I_ satisfying \(|S\cap I|=O(n^{4/3})\) and containing \(\delta^*\). A final enumeration step then computes \(\delta^*\) from \(S\cap I\) in additional _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) time. To achieve this,<tbc>

<tbc>we prove a more general result: given any interval _I_, all distances in \(S\cap I\) can be enumerated in \(O(n^{4/3}+|S\cap I|)\) time. The result follows from an _implicit biclique partition theorem_ (Theorem 4), which computes a compact representation of all distances in \(S\cap I\) in an implicit manner within _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) time. We believe this theorem may be of independent interest. For comparison, the algorithms of Katz and Sharir \[20\] and Wang and Zhao \[28\] both rely on explicit representations of the relevant distances. Their techniques require _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>log_n_) and _n_<sup>4/3</sup>2<sup>_O_(log<sup>∗</sup>_n_)</sup> time, respectively, to construct these representations. In contrast, our representation is maintained implicitly, which is crucial for acheiving the _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) running time.

### The asymmetric case.

To solve the asymmetric case \(m\neq n\), we seek to reduce the problem to the symmetric case. For several related geometric problems, such as Hopcroft’s problem \[10\], the problem of computing \(K_\delta\) \[24\], and computing many faces in line arrangements \[26\], such a reduction is relatively straightforward, and the symmetric case algorithm can be used essentially as a black box. For the distance selection problem, however, the situation appears to be more subtle. In particular, we cannot simply invoke the symmetric case algorithm as a black box and obtain the desired running time. Instead, additional ideas are needed to combine the symmetric subproblems efficiently.

One possible reason is that distance selection lacks the type of decomposability enjoyed by the above problems. Solving a subproblem on two subsets \(A'\subseteq A\) and \(B'\subseteq B\) does not immediately provide useful information for solving the original problem on _A_ and _B_. Consequently, extra care is needed in order to exploit the symmetric case machinery while acheiving the desired time complexity.

Besides distance selection, the techniques developed in this paper may also be useful for other geometric optimization problems involving interpoint distances.

### Outline.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces notation and reviews the partial biclique partition technique from \[28\]. The next three sections focus on the symmetric case _m=n_. Section 3 develops the approximate counting theorem (Theorem 1) and the resulting quasi-decision algorithm (Theorem 2). Section 4 proves the distance representation theorem (Theorem 3). Section 5 combines these ingredients to obtain a deterministic _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>)-time distance selection algorithm. Section 6 extends the framework to the asymmetric case \(m\neq n\) and presents the _O(m_log<sup>2</sup>_n+n_log<sup>2</sup>_m+m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>)-time algorithm.

## 2 Preliminaries

For any two points _a,b_ in the plane, we use \(\|ab\|\) to denote their Euclidean distance. Let _A_ and _B_ be two sets of points in the plane. Define \(S(A,B)=\{\|ab\||a\in A,b\in B\}\) to be the set of pairwise distances between points of _A_ and points of _B_. We write _S_ for _S(A,B_) when the point sets are clear from the context. We assume that no point of _A_ is co-located with a point of _B_. Consequently, \(0\notin S\).

For an interval _I_, we use \(S\cap I\) to denote the subset of distances in _S_ whose values lie in _I_. Unless stated otherwise, all intervals considered in this paper are of the form \((\alpha,\beta]\), that is, they are open on the left endpoint and closed on the right endpoint.

For any region \(\sigma\) in the plane, we use \(A(\sigma)\) to denote the subset of points of _A_ in \(\sigma\), i.e., \(A(\sigma)=A\cap\sigma\). We define \(B(\sigma)\) similarly.

**Definition 1** (Biclique)**.** _Let_ \(A_t\subseteq A\) _and_ \(B_t\subseteq B\)_. A_ biclique _is a complete bipartite graph with bipartition_ (_A<sub>t</sub>,B<sub>t</sub>), i.e., the graph containing all edges between every point of A<sub>t</sub> and every point of B<sub>t</sub>. We denote the biclique by_ \(A_t\times B_t\)_. The_ size _of the biclique is defined as_ |_A<sub>t</sub>_|+|_B<sub>t</sub>|._

A biclique \(A_t\times B_t\) compactly represents all distance pairs between points of _A<sub>t</sub>_ and points of _B<sub>t</sub>_. We therefore often say that the biclique _records_ these pairs or their corresponding distances. For a<tbc>

point \(a\in A_t\) and a point \(b\in B_t\), we call (_a,b_) a _point pair_ (or simply a _pair_) of the biclique. Two bicliques \(A_t\times B_t\) and \(A_{t^\prime}\times B_{t^\prime}\) are _edge-disjoint_ if they do not contain the same point pair.

## 2.1 Partial biclique partitions

The main tool used throughout the paper is a partial biclique partition used by Wang and Zhao \[28\] (called _partial batched range searching_ in \[28\]). Since both the approximate counting algorithm and the distance representation theorem rely heavily on this construction, we review it and derive the recurrence relations that will be used later.

Let \(I=(\alpha,\beta]\) be an interval. For every point \(a\in A\), define _D<sub>a</sub>(I_) to be the annulus centered at _a_ with inner radius \(\alpha\) and outer radius \(\beta\). When the interval _I_ is clear from the context, we simply write _D<sub>a</sub>_. We assume that the outer boundary belongs to _D<sub>a</sub>_ while the inner boundary does not. Hence, for any point \(b\in B\), \(b\in D_a\) if and only if \(\|ab\|\in(\alpha,\beta]\).

Let \(\mathcal{D}=\{D_a|a\in A\}\) be the set of all annuli centered at the points of _A_.

The purpose of a partial biclique partition is to represent all point pairs whose distances lie in a given interval by a small collection of bicliques while allowing a controlled collection of unresolved pairs.

**Definition 2** (Partial Biclique Partition)**.** _Given an interval I, a_ partial biclique partition _for A and B consists of two collections of edge-disjoint bicliques_ \(\Gamma=\{A_t\times B_t|A_t\subseteq A,B_t\subseteq B\}\) _and_ \(\Pi=\{A'_s\times B'_s|A'_s\subseteq A,B'_s\subseteq B\}\) _such that the following conditions hold._

1. _For every pair_ \((a,b)\in A_t\times B_t\in\Gamma\), \(\|ab\|\in I\).<tbc>

_2._ _For every pair of points_ \(a\in A\) _and_ \(b\in B\) _with_ \(\|ab\|\in I\)_, there exists a biclique in either_ \(\Gamma\) _or_ \(\Pi\) _that contains_ (_a,b)._

In other words, the two collections \(\Gamma\) and \(\Pi\) together record all pairs (_a,b_) with distance in _I_. Every pair recorded in a biclique of \(\Gamma\) is guaranteed to have distance in _I_, while this may not be true for the pairs recorded in \(\Pi\). For this reason, we call the pairs recorded in \(\Pi\) _uncertain pairs_, and the pairs recorded in \(\Gamma\) _certified pairs_.

The following lemma is a useful tool inherited from \[28\].

**Lemma 1** (Lemma 1 of \[28\])**.** _Let m_=|_A_| _and n_=|_B|. For any parameter_ \(1\le r\le min\{m^{1/3},n^{1/3}\}\)_, one can compute a partial biclique partition for A and B with collections_ \(\Gamma\) _and_ \(\Pi\) _in O(mr_log_r+nr_) _time such that:_

1. \(\sum_t(|A_t|+|B_t|)=O(mrlogr+nr)\).<tbc>

_2._ _For every biclique_ \(A'_s\times B'_s\in\Pi\), \(|A'_s|\le m/r^3\) _and_ \(|B'_s|\le n/r^3\).<tbc>

_3._ _The total number of uncertain pairs recorded in_ \(\Pi\) _is O(mn/r_<sup>2</sup>).

We briefly review the algorithm of Lemma 1, since it will be used repeatedly throughout the paper. Several concepts and notation introduced here will also be needed later.

### Cuttings.

Recall that D consists of _m_ annuli centered at the points of _A_, each bounded by two circles. For any compact region \(\sigma\) in the plane, let \(\mathcal{D}_\sigma\subseteq\mathcal{D}\) denote the subset of annuli whose bounding circles cross the relative interior of \(\sigma\).

For a parameter _r_ with \(1\le r\le m\), a (1_/r_)_-cutting_ for D is a collection \(\Xi\) of constant-complexity cells with pairwise disjoint interiors whose union covers the entire plane such that \(|\mathcal{D}_\sigma|\le m/r\) for every cell \(\sigma\in\Xi\). The set \(\mathcal{D}_\sigma\) is often called the _conflict list_ of \(\sigma\). The _size_ of \(\Xi\) is the number of its cells.

We say that a cutting \(\Xi'c\)_-refines_ a cutting \(\Xi\) if every cell of \(\Xi'\) is contained in a cell of \(\Xi\) and every cell of \(\Xi\) contains at most _c_ cells of \(\Xi'\).

A _hierarchical_ (1_/r)-cutting_ for D is a sequence of cuttings \(\Xi_0,\Xi_1,\dots,\Xi_k\) such that:

1. \(\Xi_ic\)-refines \(\Xi_{i-1}\) for every \(1\le i\le k\), for some constant _c_;<tbc>

2. for each \(1\le i\le k\), \(\Xi_i\) is a \((1/\rho^i)\)-cutting of size \(O(\rho^{2i})\), for some constant \(\rho\);<tbc>

3. \(\Xi_0\) consists of a single cell equal to the entire plane.

Setting \(k=\lceil log_\rho r\rceil\) makes the last cutting \(\Xi_k\) a (1_/r_)-cutting of size _O(r_<sup>2</sup>), which is also the total size of all cuttings in the hierarchy.

If a cell \(\sigma\in\Xi_i\) is contained in a cell \(\sigma'\in\Xi_{i-1}\), then \(\sigma'\) is called the _parent_ of \(\sigma\), and \(\sigma\) is called a _child_ of \(\sigma'\). In this way, the cells form a tree, called the _cutting tree_, whose root is the unique cell of \(\Xi_0\). We often use \(\Xi\) to denote the set of all cells in all cuttings in the hierarchy. We also view \(\Xi\) as the corresponding cutting tree and use the notions of ancestors and descendants.

A hierarchical (1_/r_)-cutting for D can be computed in _O(mr_) time for any \(1\le r\le m\), e.g., by the algorithm of Wang \[24\], which adapts Chazelle’s construction \[12\]. The algorithm also computes the conflict list \(\mathcal{D}_\sigma\) for every cell \(\sigma\in\Xi\). Consequently, the total size of all conflict lists is _O(mr_).

## Algorithm for Lemma 1.

We briefly review the algorithm; see \[28\] for details.

We first construct a hierarchical (1_/r_)-cutting \(\{\Xi_0,\Xi_1,\dots,\Xi_k\}\) for D, which takes _O(mr_) time. We use \(\Xi\) to denote the set of all cutting cells.

For each cell \(\sigma\in\Xi\), we compute a canonical subset \(B(\sigma)=B\cap\sigma\). This can be done in _O(n_log_r_) time by processing the points of _B_ in a top-down manner through the cutting tree. Since \(k=\Theta(logr)\), each point of _B_ is stored in _O_(log_r_) canonical subsets. Hence, the total size of all canonical subsets \(B(\sigma)\), \(\sigma\in\Xi\), is _O(n_log_r_).

Next, for each cell \(\sigma\in\Xi\), we compute another canonical subset \(A_\sigma\subseteq A\). Specifically, a point \(a\in A\) belongs to \(A_\sigma\) if the annulus _D<sub>a</sub>_ contains \(\sigma\) but does not contain the parent of \(\sigma\). Since each cell has _O_(1) children, all subsets \(A_\sigma\) can be computed in _O(mr_) time in a top-down manner. The total size of all subsets \(A_\sigma\) is also _O(mr_).

By definition, for every cell \(\sigma\in\Xi\), every pair \((a,b)\in A_\sigma\times B(\sigma)\) satisfies \(\|ab\|\in I\). Therefore, we add the biclique \(A_\sigma\times B(\sigma)\) to \(\Gamma\). The resulting bicliques are edge-disjoint. We have shown that \(\sum_{\sigma\in\Xi}|A_\sigma|=O(mr)\) and \(\sum_{\sigma\in\Xi}|B(\sigma)|=O(nlogr)\).

Consider now a cell \(\sigma\) of the last cutting \(\Xi_k\). Since \(|\mathcal{D}_\sigma|\le m/r\), define \(\hat{A}_\sigma=\{a\in A|D_a\in\mathcal{D}_\sigma\}\). We do not know whether distances between points of \(\hat{A}_\sigma\) and points of \(B(\sigma)\) lie in _I_. If \(|B(\sigma)|>n/r^2\), then we partition \(B(\sigma)\) into subsets of size between _n/_(2_r_<sup>2</sup>) and _n/r_<sup>2</sup>, called _standard subsets_. Since |_B_|=_n_ and \(\Xi_k\) contains _O(r_<sup>2</sup>) cells, the total number of standard subsets over all cells of \(\Xi_k\) is _O(r_<sup>2</sup>).

For each standard subset \(\hat{B}(\sigma)\subseteq B(\sigma)\), we form a recursive subproblem \((\hat{A}_\sigma,\hat{B}(\sigma))\). There are _O(r_<sup>2</sup>) such subproblems. Since \(|\hat{A}_\sigma|\le m/r\) and \(|\hat{B}(\sigma)|\le n/r^2\), the running time satisfies the recurrence

\(T(m,n)=O(mr+nlogr)+O(r^2)\cdot T\big(\frac{m}{r},\frac{n}{r^2}\big).\) (1)

Throughout the paper, we use _T(m,n_) interchangeably to denote both the running time and the corresponding subproblem involving two point sets of sizes _m_ and _n_.

We next solve the problem in a dual setting by switching the roles of _A_ and _B_, i.e., defining annuli centered at the points of _B_. Symmetrically, we obtain

\(T(m,n)=O(nr+mlogr)+O(r^2)\cdot T\big(\frac{m}{r^2},\frac{n}{r}\big).\) (2)

Applying (2) to each subproblem of (1) with the same parameter _r_ yields

\(T(m,n)=O(mrlogr+nr)+O(r^4)\cdot T\big(\frac{m}{r^3},\frac{n}{r^3}\big).\) (3)

The balanced recurrence implies that, in _O(mr_log_r+nr_) time, one can compute a collection of _O(r_<sup>4</sup>) edge-disjoint bicliques \(A_t\times B_t\) such that every pair \((a,b)\in A_t\times B_t\) satisfies \(\|ab\|\in I\). Furthermore, \(\sum_t(|A_t|+|B_t|)=O(mrlogr+nr)\). We return this collection as \(\Gamma\).

In addition, we obtain _O(r_<sup>4</sup>) bicliques \(A'_s\times B'_s\) corresponding to the subproblems _T(m/r_<sup>3</sup>_,n/r_<sup>3</sup>). For these bicliques, we do not know whether \(\|ab\|\in I\) for pairs \((a,b)\in A'_s\times B'_s\). We return the collection of all such bicliques as \(\Pi\). Consequently, \(|A'_s|\le m/r^3\) and \(|B'_s|\le n/r^3\) for every \(A'_s\times B'_s\in\Pi\), and the total number of uncertain pairs recorded in \(\Pi\) is _O(mn/r_<sup>2</sup>). This proves Lemma 1.

We remark that Recurrence (3) is the key algorithmic consequence of the partial biclique partition framework. It will serve as the starting point for both the approximate counting algorithm in Section 3 and the distance representation algorithm in Section 4.

## 3 Approximate counting and quasi-decision

In this section and the next two sections, we assume that |_A_|=|_B_|=_n_.

This section develops an approximate counting algorithm for interval distances. The quasi-decision theorem then follows immediately by comparing the approximate count with a given threshold.

For an interval _I_, let \(\kappa(I)=|S\cap I|\) denote the number of distances of _S_ whose values lie in _I_.

Our main goal in this section is to prove the following approximate counting theorem.

**Theorem 1** (Approximate Counting)**.** _Let I be any interval. For every integer i with_ \(1\le i\le O(log^*n)\)_, one can compute an integer_ \(\hat{\kappa}(I)\) _such that_

\(|\kappa(I)-\hat{\kappa}(I)|\le c_0\cdot n^{4/3}(log^{(i)}n)^4\)

_for some constant c_<sub>0</sub>_\>_0.

_The runtime is O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_) _for i_=1,2_, and O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_)<sup>2</sup>) _for_ \(i\ge 3\).

### Remark.

Ideally, we would like to compute \(\kappa(I)\) exactly. However, exact computation requires _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) time \[10,24\], which is optimal in a restricted computational model. The purpose of Theorem 1 is to obtain a faster algorithm by computing only an approximation of \(\kappa(I)\) while controlling the approximation error. Furthermore, the theorem provides a trade-off between running time and error: allowing a larger error leads to a faster algorithm.

Theorem 1 immediately yields the following quasi-decision theorem, which will be used later in the distance selection algorithm of Section 5.

**Theorem 2** (Quasi-Decision)**.** _Given an interval I and an integer K with_ \(1\le K\le n^2\)_, for every i with_ \(1\le i\le O(log^*n)\)_, there exists an algorithm whose output has one of the following three outcomes:_

1. _the algorithm reports_ \(\kappa(I)<K\);<tbc>

2. _the algorithm reports_ \(\kappa(I)>K\);<tbc>

_3._ _the algorithm reports "unsure", in which case_<tbc>

<tbc>\(|\kappa(I)-K|\le c_0\cdot n^{4/3}(log^{(i)}n)^4\)<tbc>

<tbc>_for some constant c_<sub>0</sub>_\>_0.<tbc>

_The algorithm runs in O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_) _time for i_=1,2_, and in O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_)<sup>2</sup>) _time for_ \(i\ge 3\).

_Proof._ Compute \(\hat{\kappa}(I)\) using Theorem 1. If \(\hat{\kappa}(I)+c_0n^{4/3}(log^{(i)}n)^4<K\), then \(\kappa(I)<K\). If \(\hat{\kappa}(I)-c_0n^{4/3}(log^{(i)}n)^4>K\), then \(\kappa(I)>K\). Otherwise, report "unsure". The correctness follows immediately from the error guarantee of Theorem 1.

In the remainder of this section, we prove Theorem 1. The proof naturally splits into two cases. For _i_=1,2, the algorithm follows directly from repeated applications of Lemma 1. The case \(i\ge 3\) is substantially more difficult and new techniques are required.

## 3.1 The cases _i_=1,2

For _i_=1,2, the approximate counting algorithm follows directly from the balanced recurrence (3). For convenience, we restate the recurrence here in the symmetric case _m=n_:

\(T(n,n)=O(nrlogr)+O(r^4)\cdot T\big(\frac{n}{r^3},\frac{n}{r^3}\big).\) (4)

The algorithm computes an approximate count \(\hat{\kappa}(I)\) by recursively applying Lemma 1. At each recursive step, we add to \(\hat{\kappa}(I)\) the number of certified pairs recorded by the bicliques in \(\Gamma\). Since every certified pair has distance in _I_, the only source of error comes from the uncertain pairs represented by \(\Pi\). Consequently, \(|\hat{\kappa}(I)-\kappa(I)|\) is bounded by the total number of uncertain pairs in the remaining recursive subproblems.

For _i_=1, we apply Lemma 1 once with _r=n_<sup>1/3</sup>/log<sup>2</sup>_n_. The runtime is _O(nr_log_r_), which is _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/log_n_), and the number of uncertain pairs is _O(n_<sup>2</sup>_/r_<sup>2</sup>)=_O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>log<sup>4</sup>_n_). This proves Theorem 1 for _i_=1.

For _i_=2, we apply Lemma 1 recursively twice. The first application again uses _r=n_<sup>1/3</sup>/log<sup>2</sup>_n_. For each biclique \(A'_s\times B'_s\in\Pi\), we apply Lemma 1 again with _r_=log<sup>2</sup>_n/_log<sup>2</sup>log_n_. The total runtime is _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/loglog_n_), while the total number of uncertain pairs after the second recursive step is _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/log<sup>4</sup>log_n_). This proves Theorem 1 for _i_=2.

## 3.2 The case \(i\ge 3\)

For \(i\ge 3\), one might try to continue applying Recurrence (4). However, every application of the recurrence introduces a constant-factor loss. After _i_ recursive levels, both the running time and the error bound would incur an extra factor 2<sup>_O(i_)</sup>. Consequently, this approach is sufficient only when _i=O_(1). To obtain the bounds stated in Theorem 1 for general _i_, a different approach is needed.

The key observation is that for approximate counting we do not need to construct all bicliques explicitly. Instead, it is sufficient to know, for each cell of the last cutting, how many annuli completely contain the cell. This allows us to count certified pairs implicitly through cutting cells rather than explicitly through bicliques.

The remaining difficulty is point location. To compute the contribution of a cell, we need to determine, for every point of _B_, the cell of the last cutting that contains it. A straightforward implementation would require logarithmic time per point. To avoid this overhead, we use the \(\Gamma\)- framework of Chan and Zheng \[10\]. The framework becomes applicable because, after two levels of recursion, the remaining subproblem size is already extremely small. The details are given below.

We consider a general \(i\ge 3\).

We first apply Recurrence (4) twice with _r=n_<sup>1/3</sup>/log<sup>2</sup>_n_, exactly as in the case _i_=2. This takes _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/loglog_n_) time and produces _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/log<sup>8</sup>_n_) certified bicliques together with _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/log<sup>8</sup>_n_) uncertain bicliques. We add \(\sum_t(|A_t|\cdot|B_t|)\) over all certified bicliques to \(\hat{\kappa}(I)\) (initially, \(\hat{\kappa}(I)=0\)). Note that the total size of all certified bicliques satisfies \(\sum_t(|A_t|+|B_t|)=O(n^{4/3}/loglogn)\).

After two recursive levels, each uncertain biclique corresponds to a subproblem _T(q,q_), where _q_=log<sup>6</sup>log_n_. Hence, the total running time satisfies

\(T(n,n)=O(n^{4/3}/\mathrm{loglog}n)+O(n^{4/3}/\mathrm{log}^8\mathrm{log}n)\cdot T(q,q).\) (5)

We next solve the subproblem _T(q,q_). Since _q_ is sufficiently small (e.g., 2<sup>poly(_q_)</sup>=_O(n_) for any polynomial function \(\mathrm{poly}(\cdot))\), we can exploit the \(\Gamma\)-framework of Chan and Zheng \[10\].

Let _g_=log<sup>(_i_-2)</sup>_q_. We first apply Recurrence (2) with _m=n=q_ and _r=q_<sup>1/3</sup>_/g_<sup>2</sup>, obtaining

\(T(q,q)=O\left(\frac{q^{4/3}}{g^2}\right)+O\left(\frac{q^{2/3}}{g^4}\right)\cdot T\big(q^{1/3}g^4,q^{2/3}g^2\big).\) (6)

As before, we add the number of certified pairs produced by the recurrence to \(\hat{\kappa}(I)\).

### Solving subproblems _T(q_<sup>1/3</sup>_g_<sup>4</sup>_,q_<sup>2/3</sup>_g_<sup>2</sup>).

We now solve the subproblem _T(q_<sup>1/3</sup>_g_<sup>4</sup>_,q_<sup>2/3</sup>_g_<sup>2</sup>), which corresponds to an uncertain biclique \(A'\times B'\) with \(A'\subseteq A\), \(B'\subseteq B\), \(|A'|\le q^{1/3}g^4\), and \(|B'|\le q^{2/3}g^2\). Let \(m'=|A'|\) and \(n'=|B'|\).

Let \(\mathcal{D}'\) be the set of annuli defined by the points of \(A'\) with respect to the interval _I_. We compute a hierarchical \((1/r')\)-cutting \(\{\Xi_0,\Xi_1,\dots,\Xi_k\}\) for \(\mathcal{D}'\), where \(r'=m'/g^6\). This takes \(O(m'r')\) time. For every cell \(\sigma\) of the last cutting \(\Xi_k\), let \(m'_\sigma\) denote the number of annuli of \(\mathcal{D}'\) that completely contain \(\sigma\). Since each cutting cell has _O_(1) children, all values \(m'_\sigma\) can be computed in \(O(m'r')\) time by traversing the cutting tree.

Next, we locate every point of \(B'\) in the last cutting \(\Xi_k\). A straightforward point location procedure would require \(O(\mathrm{log}r')\) time per point, which is not efficient enough for our purpose. To avoid this overhead, we apply the \(\Gamma\)-framework of Chan and Zheng \[10\].

Since _q_=log<sup>6</sup>log_n_, the subproblem size is sufficiently small for the framework to be effective. In a manner similar to \[10, Lemma 4.4\], each point location can be performed in amortized _O_(1) time (say, after _O(n_<sup>5/4</sup>)-time preprocessing for _A_ and _B_). Note that the point location problem in \[10, Lemma 4.4\] is on a line arrangement, whereas our point location problem is on a cutting \(\Xi_k\). Nevertheless, the same idea applies by exploiting the hierarchical structure of the cuttings; see Section 5.3 of the arXiv version of \[26\] for a similar problem.

Consequently, all point locations for the points of \(B'\) can be performed in \(O(n')\) amortized time. After that, we obtain the canonical subsets \(B'(\sigma)=B'\cap\sigma\) for all cells \(\sigma\in\Xi_k\).

For each cell \(\sigma\), we add \(m'_\sigma\cdot|B'(\sigma)|\) to \(\hat{\kappa}(I)\). This is the key difference from the cases _i_=1,2: certified pairs are counted implicitly through cutting cells rather than explicitly through bicliques.

The unresolved pairs are represented by bicliques \(\hat{A}'_\sigma\times B'(\sigma)\), where \(\hat{A}'_\sigma=\{a\in A'|D_a\in\mathcal{D}'_\sigma\}\). Since \(|\hat{A}'_\sigma|\le m'/r'\) and \(\sum_\sigma|B'(\sigma)|=n'\), the total number of unresolved pairs for the subproblem \(T(m',n')\) is \(O(m'n'/r')\). The running time of the subproblem is \(O(m'r'+n')\).

Since \(r'=m'/g^6\), \(m'\le q^{1/3}g^4\), and \(n'\le q^{2/3}g^2\), we obtain \(T(m',n')=O(q^{2/3}g^2)\), while the number of unresolved pairs is _O(q_<sup>2/3</sup>_g_<sup>8</sup>). Substituting these bounds into (6) yields _T(q,q_)=_O(q_<sup>4/3</sup>_/g_<sup>2</sup>), and the total number of unresolved pairs is _O(q_<sup>4/3</sup>_g_<sup>4</sup>).

Substituting these bounds into (5) yields _T(n,n_)=_O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>_/g_<sup>2</sup>), and the total number of unresolved pairs is _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>_g_<sup>4</sup>). Recalling that _g_=log<sup>(_i_-2)</sup>_q_, we conclude that the total running time is _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_)<sup>2</sup>), while \(|\hat{\kappa}(I)-\kappa(I)|=O(n^{4/3}(\mathrm{log}^{(i)}n)^4)\).

This proves Theorem 1 for all \(i\ge 3\).

## 4 Distance representation

The approximate counting algorithm of Section 3 is sufficient for quasi-decision. However, it does not directly yield an _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>)-time distance selection algorithm, because distance selection ultimately<tbc>

requires a compact representation of the candidate distances themselves. This section develops such a representation. The resulting theorem is the main structural result of the paper and constitutes the principal new ingredient that enables the deterministic _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>)-time algorithm.

Given an interval _I_, our goal is to represent the distances of \(S\cap I\) by a collection of bicliques. Ideally, we would like to represent all distances of \(S\cap I\). However, it is unlikely this can be achieved in time _o(n_<sup>4/3</sup>). Instead, our strategy is to represent only a constant fraction of the distances in \(S\cap I\), which is sufficient for our prune-and-search distance selection algorithm as will be shown in Section 5.

This idea is motivated by Lemma 1. The lemma already produces a compact representation of most distance pairs while leaving a controlled collection of unresolved pairs. However, the resulting algorithm is not efficient enough for our purposes. Our new algorithm goes one step further: among the certified pairs, it records only a constant fraction of them. This additional flexibility allows us to obtain a substantially faster representation algorithm.

Like the approximate counting theorem, the distance representation theorem provides a trade-off between running time and representation error. Roughly speaking, the more unresolved pairs we allow, the more efficient the algorithm becomes. For example, if no unresolved pairs are allowed, our algorithm runs in _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) time. By comparison, the technique of Wang and Zhao \[28, Theorem 1\] requires \(n^{4/3}\cdot 2^{O(log^*n)}\) time for the same task.<sup>1</sup>

The following theorem summarizes the main result of this section.

**Theorem 3** (Distance Representation)**.** _Given an interval I, for every integer i with_ \(1\le i\le O(log^*n)\) _such that_

\(|S\cap I|\ge c_1\cdot n^{4/3}(log^{(i)}n)^4\)

_for a sufficiently large constant c_<sub>1</sub>_\>_0_, one can compute a collection_ \(\Gamma=\{A_t\times B_t\}\) _of edge-disjoint bicliques such that:_

1. _every pair recorded by a biclique of_ \(\Gamma\) _has distance in I;_<tbc>

2. \(\sum_t|A_t||B_t|\ge 0.4\cdot|S\cap I|\);<tbc>

_3._ \(\sum_t(|A_t|+|B_t|)\) _is O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_) _for i_=1,2_, and O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_)<sup>2</sup>) _for_ \(i\ge 3\).

_The construction time is O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_) _for i_=1,2_, and O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_)<sup>2</sup>) _for_ \(i\ge 3\).

### Remark.

The second statement implies that the bicliques of \(\Gamma\) record at least forty percent of the distances in \(S\cap I\). Although the theorem does not explicitly mention unresolved pairs, they are an essential part of the construction.

In the remainder of this section, we prove Theorem 3. The proof follows the same high-level framework as the approximate counting algorithm. However, there is a crucial difference. Theorem 1 only requires counting target distances, whereas here we must organize them into bicliques. Consequently, the representation problem is substantially more challenging.

We begin with the easier cases _i_=1,2, where the algorithm follows directly from Lemma 1. The case \(i\ge 3\) requires new ideas and constitutes the main technical contribution of this section.

## 4.1 The cases _i_=1,2

For _i_=1,2, the distance representation theorem follows directly from the recursive construction underlying Theorem 1.

<sup>1</sup>One may wonder whether the \(\Gamma\)-framework \[10\] can be used to remove the 2<sup>_O_(log<sup>∗</sup>_n_)</sup> factor. It is not clear to us whether this is possible. See the discussion in \[28\] about this challenge following Theorem 1.

As in Section 3.1, every certified biclique produced by Recurrence (4) is added to \(\Gamma\), while the bicliques corresponding to the remaining recursive subproblems form \(\Pi\).

For _i_=1, we apply Lemma 1 once with _r=n_<sup>1/3</sup>/log<sup>2</sup>_n_. The running time is _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/log_n_), and \(\sum_t(|A_t|+|B_t|)=O(n^{4/3}/\mathrm{log}n)\). The total number of uncertain pairs recorded in \(\Pi\) is _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>log<sup>4</sup>_n_).

Let \(N(\Pi)\) denote the number of uncertain pairs recorded in \(\Pi\). Since all certified pairs are represented in \(\Gamma\), we have<tbc>

\(\sum_{A_t\times B_t\in\Gamma}|A_t||B_t|=|S\cap I|-N(\Pi).\)

<tbc>Since \(N(\Pi)\le cn^{4/3}\mathrm{log}^4n\) for some constant _c\>_0, and Theorem 3 assumes \(|S\cap I|\ge c_1n^{4/3}\mathrm{log}^4n\), we obtain<tbc>

\(\sum_{A_t\times B_t\in\Gamma}|A_t||B_t|\ge(1-\frac{c}{c_1})|S\cap I|.\)

<tbc>Therefore, by choosing _c_<sub>1</sub> sufficiently large, we have

\(\sum_{A_t\times B_t\in\Gamma}|A_t||B_t|\ge 0.4|S\cap I|.\)

This proves the theorem for _i_=1.

For _i_=2, we apply Recurrence (4) twice. As shown in Section 3.1, the running time becomes _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/loglog_n_), while the total number of uncertain pairs is _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>log<sup>4</sup>log_n_). Again, all certified pairs are recorded in \(\Gamma\), and therefore \(\sum_{A_t\times B_t\in\Gamma}|A_t||B_t|=|S\cap I|-N(\Pi)\). Using the assumption \(|S\cap I|\ge c_1n^{4/3}(\mathrm{loglog}n)^4\) and choosing _c_<sub>1</sub> sufficiently large yields \(\sum_{A_t\times B_t\in\Gamma}|A_t||B_t|\ge 0.4|S\cap I|\).

The size bound \(\sum_t(|A_t|+|B_t|)=O(n^{4/3}/\mathrm{loglog}n)\) follows directly from the recurrence. This proves the theorem for _i_=2.

## 4.2 The case \(i\ge 3\)

For \(i\ge 3\), one might try to continue applying Recurrence (4). As discussed in Section 3.2, this approach incurs a constant-factor loss at every recursive level and therefore does not yield the bounds of Theorem 3 for general _i_. Consequently, a different approach is required.

The high-level framework remains the same as in Section 3.2. We again apply the recurrence twice and reduce the problem to a collection of tiny subproblems _T(q,q_), where _q_=log<sup>6</sup>log_n_. However, the way we solve these subproblems is fundamentally different.

For approximate counting, it suffices to know, for each cell of the last cutting, how many annuli completely contain the cell. This allows us to count certified pairs without explicitly constructing bicliques. For distance representation, however, this information is no longer sufficient. We must explicitly organize the target pairs into bicliques, and therefore a new idea is needed.

We follow the same notation as in Section 3.2 and obtain Recurrence (5). We add all certified bicliques produced during the first two recursive levels to \(\Gamma\). This takes _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/loglog_n_) time, and the total contribution to \(\sum_t(|A_t|+|B_t|)\) is bounded by the same bound.

Next, for every subproblem _T(q,q_), we apply Recurrence (6) and again add all certified bicliques to \(\Gamma\). This contributes _O(q_<sup>4/3</sup>_/g_<sup>2</sup>) time and the same asymptotic amount to the total representation size.

We now solve the subproblem _T(q_<sup>1/3</sup>_g_<sup>4</sup>_,q_<sup>2/3</sup>_g_<sup>2</sup>) in Recurrence (6), which corresponds to an unresolved biclique \(A'\times B'\) with \(A'\subseteq A\), \(B'\subseteq B\), \(|A'|\le q^{1/3}g^4\), and \(|B'|\le q^{2/3}g^2\). Let \(m'=|A'|\) and \(n'=|B'|\).

Let \(\mathcal{D}'\) be the set of annuli defined by the points of \(A'\) with respect to the interval _I_. We compute a hierarchical \((1/r')\)-cutting \(\{\Xi_0,\Xi_1,\dots,\Xi_k\}\) for \(\mathcal{D}'\), where \(r'=m'/g^6\). This takes \(O(m'r')\) time. Let \(\Xi\) denote the set of all cutting cells.

In Section 3.2, the subproblem _T(q_<sup>1/3</sup>_g_<sup>4</sup>_,q_<sup>2/3</sup>_g_<sup>2</sup>) was solved by counting, for each cell of the last cutting, how many annuli completely contain the cell. That approach is sufficient for approximate counting because the goal is merely to compute a number.

For distance representation, the situation is different. We must organize the target pairs into bicliques, and therefore the numbers computed in Section 3.2 are no longer useful by themselves. To overcome this difficulty, we introduce a new notion called _capture cells_. Capture cells allow us to represent a constant fraction of the certified pairs while maintaining the desired running-time bound.

In what follows, we first define capture cells and then show how they lead to the distance representation theorem.

## 4.2.1 Capture cells

For a cell \(\sigma\in\Xi\), define \(\mathcal{A}'(\sigma)\) to be the set of points \(a\in A'\) whose annuli _D<sub>a</sub>_ completely contain \(\sigma\). We further define \(\hat{A}'_\sigma\) to be the set of points \(a\in A'\) whose annuli belong to the conflict list \(\mathcal{D}'_\sigma\).

**Definition 3.** _The inequality_ \(|\mathcal{A}'(\sigma)|\ge|\hat{A}'_\sigma|\) _is called the_ capture condition.

A cell \(\sigma\) is called a _Type-I capture cell_ if it satisfies the capture condition but its parent does not. More precisely, \(\sigma\) is a Type-I capture cell if \(|\mathcal{A}'(\sigma)|\ge|\hat{A}'_\sigma|\) and \(|\mathcal{A}'(\sigma')|<|\hat{A}'_{\sigma^\prime}|\), where \(\sigma'\) is the parent of \(\sigma\). Note that a cell of \(\Xi_0\) can never satisfy the capture condition. Indeed, \(\Xi_0\) consists of a single cell equal to the entire plane, and thus \(|\mathcal{A}'(\sigma)|=0\) while \(|\hat{A}'_\sigma|=m'\).

Recall that the cells of \(\Xi\) form a tree and the cells of the last cutting \(\Xi_k\) are _leaf cells_. We consider a cell to be both an ancestor and a descendant of itself.

A leaf cell whose root-to-leaf path contains no Type-I capture cell is called a _Type-II capture cell_.

We refer to both Type-I and Type-II cells as _capture cells_, and use \(\Sigma\) to denote the set of all capture cells.

**Lemma 2.** _Every root-to-leaf path in_ \(\Xi\) _contains exactly one capture cell._

_Proof._ The Type-II capture cells guarantee that every root-to-leaf path contains at least one capture cell. Since only leaf cells can be Type-II capture cells, it suffices to show that every root-to-leaf path contains at most one Type-I capture cell.

Let \(\sigma\) be a Type-I capture cell and let \(\sigma'\) be its parent. By definition, \(|\mathcal{A}'(\sigma')|<|\hat{A}'_{\sigma^\prime}|\).

Consider any ancestor \(\sigma''\) of \(\sigma'\). Since \(\sigma''\) contains \(\sigma'\), we have \(\hat{A}'_{\sigma^\prime}\subseteq\hat{A}'_{\sigma^{\prime\prime}}\) and therefore \(|\hat{A}'_{\sigma^\prime}|\le|\hat{A}'_{\sigma^{\prime\prime}}|\). On the other hand, \(\mathcal{A}'(\sigma'')\subseteq\mathcal{A}'(\sigma')\), and thus \(|\mathcal{A}'(\sigma'')|\le|\mathcal{A}'(\sigma')|\).

Since \(|\mathcal{A}'(\sigma')|<|\hat{A}'_{\sigma^\prime}|\), it follows that \(|\mathcal{A}'(\sigma'')|<|\hat{A}'_{\sigma^{\prime\prime}}|\). Hence, \(\sigma''\) cannot satisfy the capture condition. Therefore no ancestor of \(\sigma\) (other than \(\sigma\) itself) can be a Type-I capture cell, proving the lemma.

Lemma 2 immediately implies the following.

**Corollary 1.** _Every two capture cells have disjoint interiors._

_Proof._ By Lemma 2, two capture cells cannot belong to the same root-to-leaf path. According to the definition of the hierarchical cuttings, two cells of \(\Xi\) have overlapped interiors only if one cell is the ancestor of the other. Hence, the two capture cells cannot have overlapped interiors.

For every capture cell \(\sigma\), every pair recorded by the biclique \(\mathcal{A}'(\sigma)\times B'(\sigma)\) has distance in _I_. Let C denote the collection of all such bicliques. By Corollary 1, no point of \(B'\) belongs to two sets \(B'(\sigma)\) for two capture cells. Consequently, the bicliques of C are edge-disjoint.

We add all bicliques of C to \(\Gamma\).

Lemma 3 shows that the total size of all bicliques of C is \(O(m'r'+n')\).

**Lemma 3.** \(\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}|\mathcal{A}'(\sigma)|=O(m'r')\) _and_ \(\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}(|\mathcal{A}'(\sigma)|+|B'(\sigma)|)=O(m'r'+n')\).

_Proof._ First, since the sets \(B'(\sigma)\) are pairwise disjoint for all capture cells \(\sigma\in\Sigma\), we have \(\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}|B'(\sigma)|=O(n')\). It therefore suffices to bound \(\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}|\mathcal{A}'(\sigma)|\).

For every capture cell \(\sigma\), regardless of whether it is Type-I or Type-II, its parent \(\sigma'\) does not satisfy the capture condition. Hence, \(|\mathcal{A}'(\sigma')|<|\hat{A}'_{\sigma^\prime}|\).

Every point of \(\mathcal{A}'(\sigma)\) belongs either to \(\mathcal{A}'(\sigma')\) or to \(\hat{A}'_{\sigma^\prime}\) (but not both). Therefore<tbc>

\(|\mathcal{A}'(\sigma)|\le|\mathcal{A}'(\sigma')|+|\hat{A}'_{\sigma^\prime}|<2|\hat{A}'_{\sigma^\prime}|.\)

<tbc>Summing over all capture cells and using the fact that every cell has _O_(1) children gives

\(\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}|\mathcal{A}'(\sigma)|=O\left(\sum_{\sigma^\prime\in\Xi}|\hat{A}'_{\sigma^\prime}|\right).\)

Since the total size of the conflict lists of all cells of \(\Xi\) is \(O(m'r')\), we have \(\sum_{\sigma^\prime\in\Xi}|\hat{A}'_{\sigma^\prime}|=O(m'r')\). The lemma follows.

**Lemma 4.** _All bicliques of_ C _can be computed in_ \(O(m'r'+n')\) _time._

_Proof._ We first identify all capture cells. After the hierarchical cutting is constructed, the conflict list \(\mathcal{D}'_\sigma\) is available for every cell \(\sigma\in\Xi\), and therefore \(|\hat{A}'_\sigma|\) is also known. We traverse the cutting tree \(\Xi\) in a top-down manner while maintaining \(|\mathcal{A}'(\sigma)|\) for every cell \(\sigma\). Since each cell has _O_(1) children, all values \(|\mathcal{A}'(\sigma)|\) can be computed in \(O(m'r')\) time. Consequently, all capture cells can be identified in \(O(m'r')\) time.

Next, we compute \(\mathcal{A}'(\sigma)\) for every capture cell \(\sigma\). For each cell \(\sigma\in\Xi\), let \(A'_\sigma\) denote the set of points \(a\in A'\) such that the annulus _D<sub>a</sub>_ contains \(\sigma\) but not the parent of \(\sigma\). As discussed in the proof of Lemma 1, all sets \(A'_\sigma\) can be computed in \(O(m'r')\) time.

Observe that \(\mathcal{A}'(\sigma)\) is precisely the union of \(A'_{\sigma^\prime}\) over all ancestors \(\sigma'\) of \(\sigma\) (where a cell is considered an ancestor of itself). Thus, for every capture cell \(\sigma\), we compute \(\mathcal{A}'(\sigma)\) by taking the union of the nonempty sets \(A'_{\sigma^\prime}\) over all ancestors \(\sigma'\) of \(\sigma\). By Lemma 3, the total size of all such sets is \(O(m'r')\), so all sets \(\mathcal{A}'(\sigma)\) can be computed within the same bound.

It remains to compute \(B'(\sigma)\) for all capture cells \(\sigma\). We first locate every point \(b\in B'\) in the last cutting. As in Section 3.2, we use the \(\Gamma\)-framework and perform each point location in amortized _O_(1) time. Hence, all point locations take \(O(n')\) amortized time.

If a capture cell \(\sigma\) is a leaf cell, then \(B'(\sigma)\) is already available. Otherwise, \(B'(\sigma)\) is the union of \(B'(\sigma'')\) over all leaf descendants \(\sigma''\) of \(\sigma\). These descendants can be found by traversing the cutting tree. Therefore, all sets \(B'(\sigma)\) can be computed in \(O(n')\) time (or \(O(n'+m'r')\) if the tree traversal is included).

Combining the above steps, all bicliques of C can be computed in \(O(m'r'+n')\) time.

Combining Lemmas 3 and 4, the subproblem \(T(m',n')\) can be solved in \(O(m'r'+n')\) time, and the total size of all bicliques produced is also \(O(m'r'+n')\).

Since \(r'=m'/g^6\), \(m'\le q^{1/3}g^4\), and \(n'\le q^{2/3}g^2\), we obtain \(T(m',n')=O(q^{2/3}g^2)\). Substituting this bound into (6) yields _T(q,q_)=_O(q_<sup>4/3</sup>_/g_<sup>2</sup>). Substituting again into (5) gives _T(n,n_)=_O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>_/g_<sup>2</sup>). Re placing _g_ by log<sup>(_i_-2)</sup>_q_ with _q_=log<sup>6</sup>log_n_, we conclude that the total running time is _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_)<sup>2</sup>). By the same analysis, the total size of all bicliques in \(\Gamma\) is also _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_)<sup>2</sup>).

The running-time and representation-size bounds of Theorem 3 are now established. It remains to prove the constant-fraction guarantee, namely that the bicliques of \(\Gamma\) record at least forty percent of the distances in \(S\cap I\). We prove this in the next subsection.

## 4.2.2 Proving the constant-fraction guarantee

It remains to prove the second statement of Theorem 3, namely that

\(\sum_{A_t\times B_t\in\Gamma}|A_t||B_t|\ge 0.4|S\cap I|.\) (7)

We begin with a single subproblem \(T(m',n')\) discussed above. Let \(S'\) denote the set of all point pairs between \(A'\) and \(B'\) whose distances lie in _I_.

For each leaf cell \(\sigma\) of \(\Xi\), the pairs recorded in the biclique \(\hat{A}'_\sigma\times B'(\sigma)\) are considered _uncertain pairs_. All other pairs of \(S'\) are called _certified pairs_. Since \(|\hat{A}'_\sigma|\le m'/r'\) and \(\sum_{\sigma\in\Xi_k}B'(\sigma)=n'\), the total number of uncertain pairs in the subproblem is \(O(m'n'/r')\).

The following lemma is the key ingredient. Its proof relies crucially on the capture condition.

**Lemma 5.** _The number of pairs recorded in the bicliques of_ C _is at least one half of all certified pairs of_ \(S'\).

_Proof._ Consider a certified pair \((a,b)\in S'\). Let \(\sigma_b\) be the leaf cell of \(\Xi\) containing _b_. Since (_a,b_) is certified, the annulus _D<sub>a</sub>_ contains \(\sigma_b\).

Assume that (_a,b_) is not recorded by any biclique of C. Then \(\sigma_b\) cannot itself be a capture cell. By Lemma 2, there is a unique capture cell \(\sigma\) on the root-to-leaf path from the root to \(\sigma_b\). Since \(\sigma_b\) is not a capture cell, \(\sigma\) must be a Type-I capture cell. Because \(b\in\sigma_b\subseteq\sigma\), we have \(b\in B'(\sigma)\).

Because (_a,b_) is not recorded by the biclique \(\mathcal{A}'(\sigma)\times B'(\sigma)\), the annulus _D<sub>a</sub>_ does not contain \(\sigma\). Since _D<sub>a</sub>_ contains \(\sigma_b\subseteq\sigma\), the boundary of _D<sub>a</sub>_ must cross \(\sigma\). Hence \(a\in\hat{A}'_\sigma\).

We charge (_a,b_) to the Type-I capture cell \(\sigma\).

The number of charged pairs associated with \(\sigma\) is at most \(|\hat{A}'_\sigma|\cdot|B'(\sigma)|\). On the other hand, the number of pairs recorded by the biclique \(\mathcal{A}'(\sigma)\times B'(\sigma)\) is \(|\mathcal{A}'(\sigma)|\cdot|B'(\sigma)|\). Since \(\sigma\) is a Type-I capture cell, \(|\mathcal{A}'(\sigma)|\ge|\hat{A}'_\sigma|\). Therefore, \(|\mathcal{A}'(\sigma)|\cdot|B'(\sigma)|\ge|\hat{A}'_\sigma|\cdot|B'(\sigma)|\). Thus every charged pair associated with \(\sigma\) can be injectively assigned to a pair recorded by \(\mathcal{A}'(\sigma)\times B'(\sigma)\).

Summing over all Type-I capture cells, the total number of recorded pairs in C is at least the total number of charged pairs. Consequently, the recorded pairs in C account for at least one half of all certified pairs of \(S'\).

We now prove (7).

Let _N_ denote the total number of uncertain pairs produced by the algorithm. As shown above, the number of uncertain pairs for a subproblem \(T(m',n')\) is \(O(m'n'/r')\), which is _O_(_q_<sup>2/3</sup>_g_<sup>8</sup>) because \(r'=m'/g^6\) and \(n'\le q^{2/3}g^2\). It follows that the number of uncertain pairs associated with a subproblem _T(q,q_) in Recurrence (6) is _O(q_<sup>4/3</sup>_g_<sup>4</sup>). Since _g_=log<sup>(_i_-2)</sup>_q_ and _q_=log<sup>6</sup>log_n_, the total number of uncertain pairs in the entire algorithm is _N=O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_)<sup>4</sup>). Hence, for some constant _c\>_0, \(N\le c\cdot n^{4/3}(log^{(i)}n)^4\). By the assumption of Theorem 3, \(|S\cap I|\ge c_1\cdot n^{4/3}(log^{(i)}n)^4\). Therefore,

\(N\le\frac{c}{c_1}|S\cap I|.\)

Let _M_ denote the number of pairs recorded in \(\Gamma\), i.e., \(M=\sum_{A_t\times B_t\in\Gamma}|A_t||B_t|\).

Partition _M_ into two parts:

• _M_<sub>1</sub>: the number of pairs recorded by bicliques produced before the subproblems \(T(m',n')\);<tbc>

• _M_<sub>2</sub>: the number of pairs recorded by the capture-cell bicliques produced inside the subproblems \(T(m',n')\).

Hence _M=M_<sub>1</sub>+_M_<sub>2</sub>.

Every pair of \(S\cap I\) belongs to exactly one of the following categories:

1. it is already recorded by the bicliques contributing to _M_<sub>1</sub>;<tbc>

2. it belongs to a certified pair inside some subproblem \(T(m',n')\);<tbc>

3. it is an uncertain pair.

<tbc>By Lemma 5, the bicliques contributing to _M_<sub>2</sub> record at least one half of all certified pairs inside the subproblems. Therefore,<tbc>

\(M_2\ge\frac{|S\cap I|-M_1-N}{2}.\)

<tbc>Using _M=M_<sub>1</sub>+_M_<sub>2</sub>, we obtain<tbc>

\(M=M_1+M_2\ge M_1+\frac{|S\cap I|-M_1-N}{2}=\frac{M_1+|S\cap I|-N}{2}\ge\frac{|S\cap I|-N}{2}.\)

<tbc>Since \(N\le(c/c_1)|S\cap I|\),

\(M\ge\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{c}{c_1}\right)|S\cap I|.\)

Choosing \(c_1\ge 5c\) yields \(M\ge 0.4|S\cap I|\). This proves (7). Together with the running-time and representation-size bounds established earlier, this completes the proof of Theorem 3.

## 5 Distance selection

In this section, we combine the quasi-decision theorem (Theorem 2) and the distance representation theorem (Theorem 3) to obtain a deterministic _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>)-time algorithm for distance selection.

Recall that \(S=\{\|ab\|:a\in A,b\in B\}\). Given an integer _K_, our goal is to compute the _K_-th smallest distance in _S_, denoted by \(\delta^*\).

The algorithm proceeds in phases. Throughout the execution, we maintain an interval _I_ containing \(\delta^*\). For _i_=1,2_,...,O_(log<sup>∗</sup>_n_), the goal of the _i_-th phase is to transform an interval _I_ satisfying<tbc>

\(|S\cap I|=O\big(n^{4/3}(log^{(i-1)}n)^4\big)\)

<tbc>(and _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) when _i_=1) and containing \(\delta^*\) into a smaller interval \(I'\subseteq I\) such that

\(|S\cap I'|=O\big(n^{4/3}(log^{(i)}n)^4\big)\)

and \(\delta^*\in I'\).

Initially, we have \(I=(0,+\infty)\), and hence \(|S\cap I|=O(n^2)\). After _O_(log<sup>∗</sup>_n_) phases, we obtain an interval _I_ satisfying \(|S\cap I|=O(n^{4/3})\) and containing \(\delta^*\). A final _distance-reporting_ step then computes \(\delta^*\) from \(S\cap I\) in additional _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) time.

We will show that the _i_-th phase consists of _O_(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_) iterations. Each iteration, which reduces the remaining candidate distances by a constant fraction, takes _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_) time for _i_=1,2, and _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_)<sup>2</sup>) time for \(i\ge 3\). Consequently, each of the first two phases runs in _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) time, while the _i_-th phase for \(i\ge 3\) runs in _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_) time. Therefore, the total time spent over all phases is

\(O(n^{4/3})\cdot\left(1+\sum_{i=3}^{O(log^*n)}\frac{1}{log^{(i)}n}\right),\)

which is _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>). Including the final distance-reporting step, the overall running time remains _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>).

In what follows, we first describe the algorithm in Section 5.1 and then prove its correctness in Section 5.2.

## 5.1 Algorithm description

We describe a general _i_-th phase. Before the phase starts, we are given an interval _I_ satisfying \(|S\cap I|=O(n^{4/3}(log^{(i-1)}n)^4)\) and containing \(\delta^*\). The goal of the phase is to produce a subinterval \(I'\subseteq I\) such that \(|S\cap I'|=O(n^{4/3}(log^{(i)}n)^4)\) and \(\delta^*\in I'\).

The phase proceeds in iterations. At the beginning of the _j_-th iteration, we are given an interval _I_<sub>_j_-1</sub> containing \(\delta^*\). Initially, _I_<sub>0</sub>=_I_. Each iteration either:

1. produces a smaller interval \(I_j\subseteq I_{j-1}\) satisfying \(\delta^*\in I_j\) and \(|S\cap I_j|\le\rho|S\cap I_{j-1}|\) for some constant \(\rho<1\); or<tbc>

2. certifies that \(|S\cap I_{j-1}|=O(n^{4/3}(log^{(i)}n)^4)\), in which case the phase terminates and returns _I_<sub>_j_-1</sub> as \(I'\).

Since the phase starts with \(|S\cap I|=O(n^{4/3}(log^{(i-1)}n)^4)\), the first outcome can occur only _O_(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_) times. Hence, the phase terminates after _O_(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_) iterations.

In the following, we describe a general _j_-th iteration. For simplicity, we assume \(i\ge 3\). The cases _i_=1,2 are identical except for the running-time bounds. We will show that each iteration requires _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_)<sup>2</sup>) time.

We begin by applying Theorem 3 to the interval _I_<sub>_j_-1</sub> with parameter _i_. This produces a collection of bicliques \(\Gamma=\{A_t\times B_t\}\) in _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_)<sup>2</sup>) time. Let \(N(\Gamma)=\sum_{A_t\times B_t\in\Gamma}|A_t||B_t|\), i.e., the number of distances recorded in \(\Gamma\). Since \(\sum_t(|A_t|+|B_t|)=O(n^{4/3}/(log^{(i)}n)^2)\) by Theorem 3, the value \(N(\Gamma)\) can be computed within the same asymptotic running time.

In the remainder of the section, let _c_<sub>1</sub> denote the constant from Theorem 3.

**Lemma 6.** _If_ \(N(\Gamma)\le c_1n^{4/3}(log^{(i)}n)^4\)_, then_ \(|S\cap I_{j-1}|=O(n^{4/3}(log^{(i)}n)^4)\).

_Proof._ If \(|S\cap I_{j-1}|<c_1n^{4/3}(log^{(i)}n)^4\), the conclusion is immediate. Otherwise, Theorem 3 implies that \(N(\Gamma)\ge 0.4|S\cap I_{j-1}|\). Therefore,

\(|S\cap I_{j-1}|\le\frac{1}{0.4}N(\Gamma)\le\frac{c_1}{0.4}n^{4/3}(log^{(i)}n)^4,\)

which proves the lemma.

If \(N(\Gamma)\le c_1n^{4/3}(log^{(i)}n)^4\), Lemma 6 allows us to terminate the current phase and return _I_<sub>_j_-1</sub> as \(I'\).

Assume henceforth that \(N(\Gamma)>c_1n^{4/3}(log^{(i)}n)^4\). Since \(|S\cap I_{j-1}|\ge N(\Gamma)\), we have \(|S\cap I_{j-1}|>c_1n^{4/3}(log^{(i)}n)^4\). Consequently, by Theorem 3, \(N(\Gamma)\ge 0.4|S\cap I_{j-1}|\).

We next construct expander graphs for the bicliques of \(\Gamma\) and use them to compute a set _E_ of weighted distances. This step is essentially the same as in \[28\], which in turn follows the method in \[20\]. For completeness, we briefly sketch the construction and refer the reader to \[28, Section 3\] or \[20\] for details.

### Computing a weighted distance set _E_.

For convenience, assume that \(|A_t|\ge|B_t|\) for every biclique \(A_t\times B_t\in\Gamma\) (otherwise we could switch the names of _A<sub>t</sub>_ and _B<sub>t</sub>_). Let _m<sub>t</sub>_=|_A<sub>t</sub>_| and _n<sub>t</sub>_=|_B<sub>t</sub>_|.

Partition each _A<sub>t</sub>_ into \(g=\lfloor m_t/n_t\rfloor\) subsets _A_<sub>_t_1</sub>_,A_<sub>_t_2</sub>_,...,A<sub>tg</sub>_, each containing between _n<sub>t</sub>_ and 2_n<sub>t</sub>_ points. Each pair (_A<sub>tf</sub>,B<sub>t</sub>_), \(1\le f\le g\), defines a biclique \(A_{tf}\times B_t\). For every such biclique, we construct a _d_-regular LPS-expander graph _G<sub>tf</sub>_ on \(A_{tf}\cup B_t\) \[20, 21\], where _d_ is a sufficiently large constant to be fixed later. The graph _G<sub>tf</sub>_ has _O_(|_A<sub>tf</sub>_|+|_B<sub>t</sub>_|) edges and can be constructed within the same time bound \[20, 21\]. Let _G<sub>t</sub>_ be the union of all graphs _G<sub>tf</sub>_. Computing all graphs _G<sub>t</sub>_ takes \(O(\sum_t(|A_t|+|B_t|))=O(n^{4/3}/(log^{(i)}n)^2)\) time. The total number of edges in all graphs is bounded by the same bound.

For every edge (_a,b_) of _G<sub>t</sub>_, where \(a\in A_t\) and \(b\in B_t\), we associate the distance \(\|ab\|\). The resulting collection of distances is denoted by _E_. The size of _E_ is therefore _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_)<sup>2</sup>). Moreover, every distance of _E_ lies in the interval _I_<sub>_j_-1</sub>.

We next assign a weight to every value of _E_. The weight assignment is chosen so that the total weight of all distances of _E_ is proportional to \(N(\Gamma)\). Since every graph _G<sub>tf</sub>_ is _d_-regular, it has at most (|_A<sub>tf</sub>_|+|_B<sub>t</sub>_|)_d/_2 edges. We assign each distance contributed by _G<sub>tf</sub>_ the weight<tbc>

\(\frac{|A_{tf}||B_t|}{|A_{tf}|+|B_t|}.\)

<tbc>The total weight of all values in _E_ is therefore at most

\(\sum_{t,f}(|A_{tf}|+|B_t|)\cdot\frac{d}{2}\cdot\frac{|A_{tf}||B_t|}{|A_{tf}|+|B_t|}=\frac{d}{2}\cdot\sum_{t,f}|A_{tf}||B_t|=\frac{d}{2}\cdot N(\Gamma).\)

Recall that \(N(\Gamma)>c_1n^{4/3}(log^{(i)}n)^4\). We may assume \(N(\Gamma)\ge 16\). Furthermore, every value of _E_ has weight at most \(|A_{tf}||B_t|/(|A_{tf}|+|B_t|)\le\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{|A_{tf}||B_t|}\le\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{N(\Gamma)}\le N(\Gamma)/8\).

Using these weights, we choose values \(\delta_1<\delta_2<\cdots<\delta_h\) from _E_, where \(1\le h\le 2d\), so that they partition _I_<sub>_j_-1</sub> into _h_+1 intervals and the total weight of the values of _E_ in each interval lies between \(N(\Gamma)/4\) and \(N(\Gamma)/2\). The partition can be computed in _O_(|_E_|) time using the linear-time selection algorithm \[7\], and therefore requires _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_)<sup>2</sup>) time.

## Computing _I<sub>j</sub>_ by testing the values of _E_.

We now use the values of _E_ to compute the next interval _I<sub>j</sub>_.

Assume that \(I_{j-1}=(\alpha,\beta]\). Let \(\delta_0=\alpha\) and \(\delta_{h+1}=\beta\). For \(1\le u\le h+1\), define \(I'_u=(\delta_{u-1},\delta_u]\). Let \(\mathcal{I}=\{I'_u|1\le u\le h+1\}\). Clearly, the intervals of I form a partition of _I_<sub>_j_-1</sub>.

Ideally, we would like to identify the interval of I containing \(\delta^*\) and return it as _I<sub>j</sub>_. Previous deterministic algorithms accomplish this by repeatedly invoking an exact decision procedure, which computes, for a given value \(\delta\), the number \(K_\delta\) of distances in _S_ that are at most \(\delta\). Since \(\delta<\delta^*\) if and only if \(K_\delta<K\), such a procedure can be used to locate the interval containing \(\delta^*\).

The exact decision algorithm requires _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) time \[10, 24\]. Consequently, using it in every iteration leads to the _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>log_n_)-time algorithm of Wang and Zhao \[28\]. To achieve an _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>)-time algorithm, we instead use the quasi-decision algorithm of Theorem 2.

For every _u_, \(1\le u\le h\), we apply Theorem 2 to the interval \(I''_u=[0,\delta_u]\). Note that \(\kappa(I''_u)=K_{\delta_u}\).

Let _u_<sub>1</sub> be the largest index such that the algorithm of Theorem 2 reports \(\kappa(I''_{u_1})<K\) (implying that \(\delta_{u_1}<\delta^*\)). If no such index exists, we set _u_<sub>1</sub>=0. Since \(\delta_0=\alpha\) and \(\delta^*\in I_{j-1}=(\alpha,\beta]\), we always have \(\delta_{u_1}<\delta^*\).

Similarly, let _u_<sub>2</sub> be the smallest index such that the algorithm reports \(\kappa(I''_{u_2})>K\) (implying that \(\delta^*\le\delta_{u_2}\)). If no such index exists, we set _u_<sub>2</sub>=_h_+1. In either case, \(\delta^*\le\delta_{u_2}\).

Therefore, \(\delta^*\in(\delta_{u_1},\delta_{u_2}]\).

We terminate the current iteration and return \(I_j=(\delta_{u_1},\delta_{u_2}]\).

Since \(h\le 2d\) and _d=O_(1), only _O_(1) calls to Theorem 2 are required. Each call takes _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_)<sup>2</sup>) time. Therefore, the total running time of the iteration remains _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>/(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_)<sup>2</sup>).

The correctness of the algorithm is established by the following lemma, whose proof is given in the next subsection.

**Lemma 7.** _There exists a constant_ \(\rho\in(0,1)\) _such that_ \(|S\cap I_j|\le\rho|S\cap I_{j-1}|\).

## 5.2 Algorithm correctness: Proving Lemma 7

Let \(n_j=|S\cap I_j|\) and \(n_{j-1}=|S\cap I_{j-1}|\). Our goal is to show that \(n_j<\rho\cdot n_{j-1}\) for some constant \(\rho\in(0,1)\).

For notational convenience, let \(m_{j-1}=N(\Gamma)\), i.e., _m_<sub>_j_-1</sub> is the number of distances of \(S\cap I_{j-1}\) recorded in \(\Gamma\). Define \(m'_{j-1}\) as the number of distances of \(S\cap I_{j-1}\) not recorded in \(\Gamma\). Then \(n_{j-1}=m_{j-1}+m'_{j-1}\).

By Theorem 3, \(m_{j-1}\ge 0.4n_{j-1}\), and therefore \(m'_{j-1}\le 0.6n_{j-1}\).

Let _S<sub>j</sub>_ denote the set of distances of \(S\cap I_j\) not recorded in \(\Gamma\), and _S_<sub>_j_-1</sub> the set of distances of \(S\cap I_{j-1}\) not recorded in \(\Gamma\). Since \(I_j\subseteq I_{j-1}\), we have \(S_j\subseteq S_{j-1}\), and hence \(|S_j|\le|S_{j-1}|=m'_{j-1}\).

Define _q<sub>j</sub>_ as the number of distances of \(S\cap I_j\) recorded in \(\Gamma\). Then

\(n_j=q_j+|S_j|\le q_j+m'_{j-1}\le q_j+0.6n_{j-1}.\)

Since \(m_{j-1}\le n_{j-1}\), Lemma 7 follows immediately from the following lemma.

**Lemma 8.** _There exists a constant_ \(\rho'\in(0,0.4)\) _such that_ \(q_j\le\rho'\cdot m_{j-1}\).

### Proof of Lemma 8.

We refer to the intervals of I as _basic intervals_. Recall that \(\delta^*\in I_j\), which implies \(\delta_{u_1}<\delta_{u_2}\) and therefore _u_<sub>1</sub>_\<u_<sub>2</sub>.

If _u_<sub>1</sub>=_u_<sub>2</sub>-1, then _I<sub>j</sub>_ consists of the single basic interval \(I'_{u_1+1}\). If _u_<sub>1</sub>=_u_<sub>2</sub>-2, then _I<sub>j</sub>_ consists of the two basic intervals \(I'_{u_1+1}\) and \(I'_{u_2}\). Otherwise, _u_<sub>1</sub>_\<u_<sub>2</sub>-2, and _I<sub>j</sub>_ can be partitioned into three intervals: \(I'_{u_1+1}\), \((\delta_{u_1+1},\delta_{u_2-1}]\), and \(I'_{u_2}\). In the following, we only analyze the third case (i.e., _u_<sub>1</sub>_\<u_<sub>2</sub>-2) since it is the most general case and the other two cases can be analyzed similarly but in a much easier way.

Let \(\hat{I}=(\delta_{u_1+1},\delta_{u_2-1}]\), and define \(\Delta=c_0\cdot n^{4/3}(log^{(i)}n)^4\), which is the term in Theorem 2(3).

**Lemma 9** (Middle interval bound)**.** \(|S\cap\hat{I}|\le 2\Delta\).

_Proof._ Since _u_<sub>1</sub>_\<u_<sub>1</sub>+1_\<u_<sub>2</sub>-1_\<u_<sub>2</sub>, the definition of _u_<sub>1</sub> implies that the quasi-decision algorithm of Theorem 2 reports "unsure" on \(I''_{u_1+1}=[0,\delta_{u_1+1}]\). Therefore, \(|\kappa(I''_{u_1+1})-K|\le\Delta\).

Similarly, the algorithm reports "unsure" on \(I''_{u_2-1}=[0,\delta_{u_2-1}]\), and thus \(|\kappa(I''_{u_2-1})-K|\le\Delta\).

Consequently,

\(|S\cap\hat{I}|=\kappa(I''_{u_2-1})-\kappa(I''_{u_1+1})\le 2\Delta.\)

The lemma thus follows.

Let _I_<sup>∗</sup> be the union of the two boundary basic intervals \(I'_{u_1+1}\) and \(I'_{u_2}\). Let \(S(\Gamma)\) denote the set of distances recorded in \(\Gamma\). Since \(\hat{I}\) and _I_<sup>∗</sup> form a partition of _I<sub>j</sub>_,

\(q_j=|S(\Gamma)\cap\hat{I}|+|S(\Gamma)\cap I'|.\) (8)

The first term is controlled by Lemma 9, while the second term will be bounded using the expander analysis.

By Lemma 9,

\(|S(\Gamma)\cap\hat{I}|\le|S\cap\hat{I}|\le 2\Delta=2c_0\cdot n^{4/3}(log^{(i)}n)^4.\)

Since _m_<sub>_j_-1</sub>_\>c_<sub>1</sub>_n_<sup>4/3</sup>(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_n_)<sup>4</sup>, we obtain

\(|S(\Gamma)\cap\hat{I}|<\frac{2c_0}{c_1}m_{j-1}.\) (9)

To bound the second term of (8), we use the following lemma.

**Lemma 10.** _There exists a constant_ \(\rho''\in(0,0.18)\) _such that_ \(|S(\Gamma)\cap I''|<\rho''m_{j-1}\) _for every basic interval_ \(I''\) _of I_<sup>∗</sup>.

_Proof._ The proof follows the previous work \[20, 28\].

Consider a graph _G<sub>tf</sub>_ computed from (_A<sub>tf</sub>,B<sub>t</sub>_) in our algorithm, where \(1\le f\le g\). Some edges of _G<sub>tf</sub>_ contribute distances in _E_. We partition all such graphs _G<sub>tf</sub>_ into two sets. Let G<sub>1</sub> denote the set of graphs _G<sub>tf</sub>_ that contribute fewer than 3(|_A<sub>tf</sub>_|+|_B<sub>t</sub>_|) distances in \(E\cap I''\), and let G<sub>2</sub> denote the set of the remaining graphs.

## The set G<sub>1</sub>.

Let \(I''=(\delta',\delta'']\). For a graph \(G_{tf}\in\mathcal{G}_1\), built on the pair (_A<sub>tf</sub>,B<sub>t</sub>_), let D_<sub>tf</sub>_ be the set of annuli centered at the points of _A<sub>tf</sub>_ with radii \(\delta'\) and \(\delta''\). Consider a 1_/r_-cutting \(\Xi\) for D_<sub>tf</sub>_, where _r_ is a constant to be chosen later. The cutting partitions the plane into _O(r_<sup>2</sup>) cells so that, for every cell \(\sigma\), at most |D_<sub>tf</sub>|/r_ annuli in D_<sub>tf</sub>_ have a boundary circle intersecting the interior of \(\sigma\).

For each cell \(\sigma\in\Xi\), let \(B_t(\sigma)\) denote the points of _B<sub>t</sub>_ inside \(\sigma\), let \(A_{tf}(\sigma)\) be the points of _A<sub>tf</sub>_ whose annuli fully contain \(\sigma\), and let \(A'_{tf}(\sigma)\) be the points of _A<sub>tf</sub>_ whose annuli have at least one boundary circle intersecting \(\sigma\). Let _N<sub>tf</sub>_ denote the number of interpoint distances between _A<sub>tf</sub>_ and _B<sub>t</sub>_ that lie in \(I''\). Then<tbc>

\(N_{tf}\le\sum_{\sigma\in\Xi}|A_{tf}(\sigma)||B_t(\sigma)|+\sum_{\sigma\in\Xi}|A'_{tf}(\sigma)||B_t(\sigma)|.\)

<tbc>Since \(|A'_{tf}(\sigma)|\le|A_{tf}|/r\) and \(\sum_{\sigma\in\Xi}|B_t(\sigma)|=|B_t|\), we obtain<tbc>

\(\sum_{\sigma\in\Xi}|A'_{tf}(\sigma)||B_t(\sigma)|=O\big(\frac{|A_{tf}||B_t|}{r}\big).\)

<tbc>Now consider \(\sum_{\sigma\in\Xi}|A_{tf}(\sigma)||B_t(\sigma)|\). Note that for any \(a\in A_{tf}(\sigma)\) and \(b\in B_t(\sigma)\), we have \(\|ab\|\in I''\). If the edge (_a,b_) exists in _G<sub>tf</sub>_, then \(\|ab\|\) must lie in \(E\cap I''\). Since \(G_{tf}\in\mathcal{G}_1\), it has fewer than 3(|_A<sub>tf</sub>_|+|_B<sub>t</sub>_|) such edges. By \[20, Corollary 2.5\], if _X_ and _Y_ are two vertex subsets of a _d_-regular expander graph on _M_ vertices and there are fewer than 3_M_ edges between _X_ and _Y_ , then \(|X||Y|\le 9M^2/d\). Applying this with \(X=A_{tf}(\sigma)\), \(Y=B_t(\sigma)\), and _M_=|_A<sub>tf</sub>_|+|_B<sub>t</sub>_|, we get<tbc>

\(\sum_{\sigma\in\Xi}|A_{tf}(\sigma)||B_t(\sigma)|\le O(r^2)\cdot\frac{9(|A_{tf}|+|B_t|)^2}{d}=O\big(\frac{r^2(|A_{tf}|+|B_t|)^2}{d}\big).\)

<tbc>Therefore,<tbc>

\(N_{tf}=O\big(\frac{|A_{tf}||B_t|}{r}\big)+O\big(\frac{r^2(|A_{tf}|+|B_t|)^2}{d}\big).\)

<tbc>Since \(|B_t|\le|A_{tf}|\le 2|B_t|\), we have \((|A_{tf}|+|B_t|)^2\le 5|A_{tf}||B_t|\). Hence,<tbc>

\(N_{tf}=O\big(\left[\frac{1}{r}+\frac{r^2}{d}\right]|A_{tf}||B_t|\big).\)

<tbc>Choosing _r=d_<sup>1/3</sup> and taking _d_ sufficiently large, we obtain<tbc>

\(N_{tf}\le 0.01\cdot|A_{tf}||B_t|.\)

<tbc>Summing over all graphs \(G_{tf}\in\mathcal{G}_1\) gives<tbc>

\(N(\mathcal{G}_1)\le 0.01\cdot\sum_{G_{tf}\in\mathcal{G}_1}|A_{tf}||B_t|,\)

where _N_(G<sub>1</sub>) is the number of distances between points of _A<sub>tf</sub>_ and points of _B<sub>t</sub>_ that are in \(I''\) for all graphs \(G_{tf}\in\mathcal{G}_1\).

Since<tbc>

\(\sum_{G_{tf}\in\mathcal{G}_1}|A_{tf}||B_t|\le\sum_t|A_t||B_t|=m_{j-1},\)

<tbc>we conclude that \(N(\mathcal{G}_1)\le 0.01\cdot m_{j-1}\).

### The set G<sub>2</sub>.

For each \(G_{tf}\in\mathcal{G}_2\), at least 3(|_A<sub>tf</sub>_|+|_B<sub>t</sub>_|) distances in \(E\cap I''\) are contributed, and therefore _G<sub>tf</sub>_ contributes at least 3|_A<sub>tf</sub>_||_B<sub>t</sub>_| to the total weight of distances in \(E\cap I''\). Recall that the total weight of distances in \(E\cap I''\) is at most _m_<sub>_j_-1</sub>/2 by our algorithm. Hence,<tbc>

\(\sum_{G_{tf}\in\mathcal{G}_2}|A_{tf}||B_t|\le\frac{m_{j-1}}{6}.\)

<tbc>Let _N_(G<sub>2</sub>) denote the number of distances between points of _A<sub>tf</sub>_ and points of _B<sub>t</sub>_ that lie in \(I''\) for all graphs \(G_{tf}\in\mathcal{G}_2\). Then<tbc>

\(N(\mathcal{G}_2)\le\sum_{G_{tf}\in\mathcal{G}_2}|A_{tf}||B_t|\le\frac{m_{j-1}}{6}.\)

### Summary.

<tbc>By definition, \(|S(\Gamma)\cap I''|=N(\mathcal{G}_1)+N(\mathcal{G}_2)\). Since \(N(\mathcal{G}_1)\le 0.01m_{j-1}\) and \(N(\mathcal{G}_2)\le m_{j-1}/6\), we obtain

\(|S(\Gamma)\cap I''|\le\left(0.01+\frac{1}{6}\right)m_{j-1}.\)

Setting \(\rho''=0.01+1/6\), we have \(\rho''\in(0,0.18)\), and the lemma follows.

By Lemma 10, and since _I_<sup>∗</sup> consists of two basic intervals, we have

\(|S(\Gamma)\cap I'|\le 2\rho''m_{j-1}<0.36m_{j-1},\)

where \(\rho''\in(0,0.18)\).

Combining this bound with (8) and (9), we obtain

\(q_j\le\frac{2c_0}{c_1}m_{j-1}+0.36m_{j-1}.\)

Choosing _c_<sub>1</sub> sufficiently large so that \(2c_0/c_1\le 0.01\) yields \(q_j\le 0.37m_{j-1}\), which proves Lemma 8.

## 5.3 The distance-reporting step

As discussed above, after _O_(log<sup>∗</sup>_n_) phases, we are left with an interval \(I=(\alpha,\beta]\) such that \(|S\cap I|=O(n^{4/3})\) and \(\delta^*\in I\). In this distance-reporting step, we compute \(\delta^*\) in an additional _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) time.

We first compute the number of distances in _S_ that are at most \(\alpha\), which can be done in _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) time \[24\]. Let \(K_\alpha\) denote this number. Our goal is then to find the \(K'\)-th smallest distance in \(S\cap I\), where \(K'=K-K_\alpha\). To this end, we first explicitly enumerate all distances in \(S\cap I\), and then apply the linear-time selection algorithm to compute \(\delta^*\). Since \(|S\cap I|=O(n^{4/3})\), the selection step takes _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) time. Therefore, the remaining task is to enumerate \(S\cap I\) within the same time bound.

A natural approach is to apply Lemma 1 to compute \(\Gamma\) and \(\Pi\) with \(\Pi=\emptyset\). We refer to this as a _full biclique partition_ (called _full batched range searching_ in \[28\]). Since \(\Pi=\emptyset\), the bicliques in \(\Gamma\) record all distances in \(S\cap I\), and thus all such distances can be enumerated from \(\Gamma\) in additional \(O(|S\cap I|)\) time. To compute a full biclique partition, the algorithm of \[28\] recursively applies Lemma 1. However, the resulting running time is \(n^{4/3}\cdot 2^{O(\mathrm{log}^*n)}\) because of the constant-factor blowup in the recurrence \[28\]. Moreover, the bound obtained in \[28\] for \(\sum_{A_t\times B_t\in\Gamma}(|A_t|+|B_t|)\) is also \(n^{4/3}\cdot 2^{O(\mathrm{log}^*n)}\), again due to the constant-factor blowup.

## Implicit biclique partition.

To obtain an _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>)-time algorithm for enumerating \(S\cap I\), one would ideally compute a full biclique partition \(\Gamma=\{A_t\times B_t\}\) in _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) time such that \(\sum_t(|A_t|+|B_t|)=O(n^{4/3})\). We achieve a weaker form of this goal in which the sets _A<sub>t</sub>_ are represented only implicitly.

Specifically, our algorithm outputs the sets _B<sub>t</sub>_ explicitly, together with a collection A of explicitly represented subsets \(A'_s\subseteq A\).
