For each _B<sub>t</sub>_, the algorithm also outputs a subcollection \(\mathcal{A}_t\subseteq\mathcal{A}\) such that the sets in A_<sub>t</sub>_ form a partition of _A<sub>t</sub>_. In particular, \(A_t=\cup_{A_s^\prime\in\mathcal{A}_t}A'_s\). Furthermore, given _B<sub>t</sub>_, the sets of A_<sub>t</sub>_ can be accessed one at a time in _O_(1) time per set. Consequently, the points of _A<sub>t</sub>_ can be enumerated in _O_(|_A<sub>t</sub>_|) time. We refer to the pair \((\Gamma,\mathcal{A})\) as an _implicit full biclique partition_ of \(S\cap I\). Our main result is stated below.

**Theorem 4** (Implicit biclique partition)**.** _Given an interval I, one can compute an implicit full biclique partition of_ \(S\cap I\) _in O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) _time._

_The output consists of a collection_ A _of subsets_ \(A'_s\subseteq A\) _and a collection_ \(\Gamma\) _of edge-disjoint bicliques_ \(A_t\times B_t\) _that together record all distances in_ \(S\cap I\)_. The sets_ \(B_t\subseteq B\) _are represented explicitly, whereas each set_ \(A_t\subseteq A\) _is represented implicitly as follows. For every biclique_ \(A_t\times B_t\)_, there is an associated subcollection_ \(\mathcal{A}_t\subseteq\mathcal{A}\) _containing O_(logloglog_n_) _subsets_ \(A'_s\)_, and these subsets form a partition of A<sub>t</sub>. Moreover, the elements of_ A_<sub>t</sub> can be accessed one at a time in O_(1) _time per element._

_Finally,_

\(\sum_{A_t\times B_t\in\Gamma}|B_t|=O(n^{4/3})\text{\textit{and}}\sum_{A_s^\prime\in\mathcal{A}}|A'_s|=O(n^{4/3}).\)

_Proof._ We run the algorithm of Lemma 1 from Section 2.1 with _m=n_. Whenever the algorithm reaches Recurrence (1), for each cell \(\sigma\in\Xi\) we add the biclique \(A_\sigma\times B_\sigma\) to \(\Gamma\), add \(A_\sigma\) to A as a subset \(A'_s\), and define \(\mathcal{A}_\sigma=\{A_\sigma\}\). Thus \(\mathcal{A}_\sigma\) contains exactly one subset.

We then continue with the dual algorithm and obtain Recurrence (2). We update \(\Gamma\) and A analogously for the dual subproblems. In this way we obtain Recurrence (3). Note that these additional bookkeeping operations do not affect the asymptotic running time, so the recurrence remains unchanged. Setting _r=n_<sup>1/3</sup>/log<sup>2</sup>_n_ yields Recurrence (5).

To solve _T(q,q_), unlike in Section 3.2, we do not use the parameter _g_ (or equivalently, we set _g_=1). Applying the algorithm corresponding to Recurrence (2) with _m=n=q_ and _r=q_<sup>1/3</sup>, we obtain

\(T(q,q)=O(q^{4/3})+O(q^{2/3})\cdot T(q^{1/3},q^{2/3}).\) (10)

As before, every biclique generated during this step is inserted into \(\Gamma\), and its associated subset is inserted into A. At this stage, each biclique \(A_t\times B_t\in\Gamma\) is associated with a single subset \(A'_s\in\mathcal{A}\).

We next consider a subproblem \(T(m',n')\) arising from Recurrence (10), where \(m'\le q^{1/3}\) and \(n'\le q^{2/3}\). Let \(A'\subseteq A\) and \(B'\subseteq B\) denote the corresponding point sets.

Let \(\mathcal{D}'\) be the set of annuli defined by the points of \(A'\) with respect to the interval _I_. We construct a hierarchical \((1/r')\)-cutting \(\{\Xi_0,\Xi_1,\dots,\Xi_k\}\) for \(\mathcal{D}'\), with \(r'=m'\). This takes \(O(m'r')\) time. Since \(r'=m'\), we can assume that every cell in the last cutting \(\Xi_k\) has an empty conflict list. Equivalently, no annulus of \(\mathcal{D}'\) has a boundary circle intersecting the interior of such a cell. Consequently, there are no uncertain pairs, which will allow us to obtain a full biclique partition.

Let \(\Xi\) denote the set of all cells in the hierarchical cutting. For each cell \(\sigma\in\Xi\), define the canonical subset \(A'_\sigma\) exactly as in Lemma 1: a point \(a\in A'\) belongs to \(A'_\sigma\) if the annulus _D<sub>a</sub>_ contains \(\sigma\) but does not contain the parent of \(\sigma\). We insert each nonempty subset \(A'_\sigma\) into A. All canonical subsets can be computed in \(O(m'r')\) time.

In addition, for every cell \(\sigma\in\Xi\) with \(A'_\sigma\neq\emptyset\), for a reason to be clear later, we store an _ancestor link_ from \(\sigma\) to its lowest ancestor \(\sigma'\) satisfying \(\sigma'\neq\sigma\) and \(A'_{\sigma^\prime}\neq\emptyset\). These links can be established in \(O(m'r')\) time by traversing the cutting tree.

Next, for each point \(b\in B'\), we determine the cell of \(\Xi_k\) containing _b_. Using the \(\Gamma\)-algorithm framework \[10\], as discussed in Section 3.2, this can be done in \(O(n')\) amortized time for all points \(b\in B'\).

For each cell \(\sigma\in\Xi_k\), let \(B_t=B'(\sigma)\), and let _A<sub>t</sub>_ be the union of all canonical subsets \(A'_{\sigma^\prime}\) over the ancestors \(\sigma'\) of \(\sigma\). We add the biclique \(A_t\times B_t\) to \(\Gamma\). We define A_<sub>t</sub>_ to be the collection of all nonempty canonical subsets \(A'_{\sigma^\prime}\) corresponding to ancestors \(\sigma'\) of \(\sigma\). By following the ancestor links, the elements of A_<sub>t</sub>_ can be accessed one at a time in _O_(1) time per element. Since the height of the cutting tree is \(O(logr')\), we have \(|\mathcal{A}_t|=O(logr')\). Further, since \(r'=m'\le q^{1/3}\) and _q=O_(log<sup>6</sup>log_n_), it follows that |A_<sub>t</sub>_|=_O_(loglog_n_).

The bicliques generated above for the cells \(\sigma\) of \(\Xi_k\) form a full biclique partition for all distances between points of \(A'\) and points of \(B'\). Therefore, the total running time for the subproblem \(T(m',n')\) is \(O(m'r'+n')\). Since \(r'=m'\), \(m'\le q^{1/3}\), and \(n'\le q^{2/3}\), we have

\(T(m',n')=O(m'^2+n')=O(q^{2/3}).\)

Substituting this bound into (10) yields _T(q,q_)=_O(q_<sup>4/3</sup>). Finally, substituting this bound into Recurrence (5) gives _T(n,n_)=_O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>), which proves Theorem 4.

**Corollary 2.** _Given an interval I, one can explicitly enumerate all distances in_ \(S\cap I\) _in_ \(O(n^{4/3}+|S\cap I|)\) _time._

_Proof._ Apply Theorem 4. For each biclique \(A_t\times B_t\in\Gamma\), we first enumerate the points of _A<sub>t</sub>_ in _O_(|_A<sub>t</sub>_|) time using its implicit representation. Then, for every \(a\in A_t\) and \(b\in B_t\), we output the distance \(\|ab\|\). By Theorem 4,

\(\sum_{A_t\times B_t\in\Gamma}|B_t|=O(n^{4/3})\text{and}\sum_{A_s^\prime\in\mathcal{A}}|A'_s|=O(n^{4/3}).\)

Hence the total overhead for recovering all sets _A<sub>t</sub>_ is _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>), while the time spent outputting distances is proportional to the number of distances reported, namely \(|S\cap I|\). Therefore, the overall running time is \(O(n^{4/3}+|S\cap I|)\).

By Corollary 2, our original problem of enumerating all distances of \(S\cap I\) can be solved in _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) time, since \(|S\cap I|=O(n^{4/3})\).

### Wrapping things up.

We have shown that \(\delta^*\) can be computed in _O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) deterministic time. Note that the algorithm of Corollary 2 can also report, together with each distance, the corresponding pair of points that realizes it. Therefore, a point pair whose distance is equal to \(\delta^*\) can be reported within the same time bound.

The following theorem summarizes our main result.

**Theorem 5.** _Given two sets A and B, each consisting of n points in the plane, and an integer K with_ \(1\le K\le n^2\)_, one can compute the K-th smallest distance among all interpoint distances between A and B in O(n_<sup>4/3</sup>) _deterministic time._

## 6 The asymmetric case

In this section, we consider the asymmetric version of the distance selection problem, where the sizes of the two point sets are not necessarily equal. Let _m_=|_A_| and _n_=|_B_|.

Our main result is the following.

**Theorem 6.** _Given a set A of m points and a set B of n points in the plane, and an integer K with_ \(1\le K\le mn\)_, one can compute the K-th smallest distance among all interpoint distances between A and B in O(n_log<sup>2</sup>_m+m_log<sup>2</sup>_n+m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>) _deterministic time._

Most of the techniques developed for the symmetric case continue to apply. We therefore only highlight the new ideas and refer to the previous sections whenever the analysis is identical. However, certain care must be taken in order to achieve the claimed complexity. We use the same notation as before, including _S_, D, \(\delta^*\), _K_, \(K_\delta\), and \(\kappa(I)\).

Without loss of generality, assume \(m\le n\). We distinguish two cases.

• If \(n\ge m^2\), we give an _O(n_log<sup>2</sup>_m_)-time algorithm.<tbc>

• If _n\<m_<sup>2</sup>, we give an algorithm running in _O(n_log<sup>2</sup>_m+m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>) time.<tbc>

<tbc>Combining the two cases yields _O(n_log<sup>2</sup>_m+m_log<sup>2</sup>_n+m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>) time for arbitrary _m_ and _n_. We begin with the easier case \(n\ge m^2\).

## 6.1 The case \(n\ge m^2\)

Throughout this subsection, we assume \(n\ge m^2\).

We begin with the following exact counting lemma.

**Lemma 11.** _Suppose that_ \(n\ge m^2\)_. Given an interval I, one can compute_ \(\kappa(I)\) _in O(n_log_m_) _time._

_Proof._ Let D denote the set of annuli defined by the points of _A_ with respect to the interval _I_.

Construct a hierarchical (1_/r_)-cutting \(\{\Xi_0,\Xi_1,\dots,\Xi_k\}\) for D with _r=m_. The construction takes _O(mr_) time. Since _r=m_, we can assume that every cell of the last cutting \(\Xi_k\) has an empty conflict list. Consequently, no annulus of D has a boundary circle intersecting the interior of any cell of \(\Xi_k\).

For every cell \(\sigma\in\Xi_k\), compute \(B(\sigma)=B\cap\sigma\). This takes _O(n_log_r_) time over all cells.

Next, compute for every cell \(\sigma\in\Xi_k\) the number \(m_\sigma\) of annuli of D that completely contain \(\sigma\). As in Section 3.2, all values \(m_\sigma\) can be computed in _O(mr_) time.

Notice that

\(\kappa(I)=\sum_{\sigma\in\Xi_k}m_\sigma|B(\sigma)|.\)

Therefore, after computing \(m_\sigma\) and \(B(\sigma)\) for all cells \(\sigma\in\Xi_k\), \(\kappa(I)\) can be readily obtained. The total running time is _O(mr+n_log_r_), which is _O(n_log_m_) since _r=m_ and \(n\ge m^2\).

By Lemma 11, given any value \(\delta\), we can determine whether \(\delta<\delta^*\) in _O(n_log_m_) time.

We now describe the distance selection algorithm.

### Overview.

The algorithm maintains an interval _I_ containing \(\delta^*\). The distances in \(S\cap I\) are called the _candidate distances_. In each iteration, we shrink _I_ so that the number of candidate distances decreases by a constant factor. Initially, \(I=(0,+\infty)\), and therefore \(|S\cap I|=O(mn)\). After _O_(log_m_) iterations, each taking _O(n_log_m_) time, we obtain an interval _I_ satisfying \(|S\cap I|=O(n)\) and containing \(\delta^*\). The total time of all iterations is thus _O(n_log<sup>2</sup>_m_). Finally, we apply a distance-reporting step that enumerates all distances in \(S\cap I\) and computes \(\delta^*\) in additional _O(n_log_m_) time.

### A general _j_-th iteration.

Suppose we are given an interval _I_<sub>_j_-1</sub>. The goal is to compute an interval _I<sub>j</sub>_ such that either

1. \(|S\cap I_j|=O(n)\), in which case we proceed to the distance-reporting step; or<tbc>

2. \(|S\cap I_j|\le\rho|S\cap I_{j-1}|\) for some constant \(\rho<1\).

We first compute \(\kappa(I_{j-1})\) using Lemma 11. If \(\kappa(I_{j-1})\le cn\) for a sufficiently large constant _c_, then \(|S\cap I_{j-1}|=O(n)\), and we proceed directly to the distance-reporting step.

Otherwise, we compute a full biclique partition by applying the algorithm for Recurrence (1) with _r=m_. Since every cell of the last cutting has an empty conflict list, the resulting collection \(\Gamma=\{A_\sigma\times B(\sigma):\sigma\in\Xi\}\) forms a full biclique partition of \(S\cap I_{j-1}\). The construction takes _O(mr+n_log_r_) time, which is _O(n_log_m_), and the total biclique size satisfies \(\sum_{A_t\times B_t\in\Gamma}(|A_t|+|B_t|)=O(nlogm)\).

We then construct the expander graphs for the bicliques of \(\Gamma\) and form the weighted distance set _E_ exactly as in Section 5.1. This also takes _O(n_log_m_) time. Next, we partition _E_ into _O_(1) basic intervals and use Lemma 11 to identify the unique interval containing \(\delta^*\). This interval is returned as _I<sub>j</sub>_. By the same analysis as in Section 5.1 (see also \[20, 28\]), there exists a constant \(\rho<1\) such that \(|S\cap I_j|\le\rho|S\cap I_{j-1}|\). Since Lemma 11 is invoked only _O_(1) times, the total running time of the iteration is _O(n_log_m_).

### Distance-reporting.

We are given an interval _I_ containing \(\delta^*\) with \(|S\cap I|=O(n)\). The goal is to finally compute \(\delta^*\).

Assume \(I=(\alpha,\beta]\). We first compute \(K_\alpha\) using Lemma 11. Then \(\delta^*\) is the \((K-K_\alpha)\)-th smallest distance in \(S\cap I\). To enumerate all distances in \(S\cap I\), we again compute a full biclique partition \(\Gamma\) as above. This takes _O(n_log_m_) time. We then explicitly output all distances recorded in \(\Gamma\), which requires \(O(|S\cap I|)=O(n)\) additional time since \(|S\cap I|=O(n)\). Finally, we apply the linear-time selection algorithm to obtain \(\delta^*\) in _O(n_) time. The total running time of the distance-reporting step is therefore _O(n_log_m_).

We conclude that if \(n\ge m^2\), then the distance selection problem can be solved in _O(n_log<sup>2</sup>_m_) time.

### Remark.

One may wonder whether the running time can be improved further to _O(n_log_m_), for example by incorporating approximate counting. The main obstacle is point location. In each iteration, we must locate all _n_ points of _B_ in a hierarchical cutting. In our symmetric case algorithm, we were able to perform these point locations in constant amortized time by using the \(\Gamma\)-framework on sufficiently small subproblems. Here, however, the \(\Gamma\)-framework is no longer applicable. Consequently, each point location costs _O_(log_m_) time, forcing the running time of every iteration to be _O(n_log_m_).

## 6.2 The case _n\<m_<sup>2</sup>

We now consider the case _n\<m_<sup>2</sup>. As before, we follow a prune-and-search framework and maintain an interval _I_ containing \(\delta^*\). Initially, \(I=(0,+\infty)\), and therefore \(|S\cap I|=O(mn)\).

The algorithm consists of three main procedures.

1. Reduce the number of candidate distances from _O(mn_) to _O(m_<sup>2</sup>).<tbc>

2. Reduce the number of candidate distances from _O(m_<sup>2</sup>) to _O(m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>).<tbc>

3. Enumerate the remaining candidate distances and compute \(\delta^*\).

The first and third procedures are relatively straightforward. The main technical challenge lies in the second procedure.

### A standard subroutine.

A recurring step in our algorithm is to apply Recurrence (1) with _r=n/m_. We refer to this as the _standard subroutine_. Substituting _r=n/m_ into Recurrence (1) yields

\(T(m,n)=O(nlogr)+O(r^2)\cdot T(q,q),q=\frac{m^2}{n}.\) (11)

The standard subroutine runs in _O(n_log_r_) time and produces a collection \(\Gamma=\{A_t\times B_t\}\) of bicliques whose total size is _O(n_log_r_). Throughout the remainder of the section, we always use _r=n/m_, _q=m_<sup>2</sup>_/n_, and let \(N(\Gamma)\) denote the number of distances recorded by \(\Gamma\).

Since \(m\le n<m^2\), we have \(r\le m\) and therefore log_r=O_(log_m_). Consequently, the running time of the standard subroutine is _O(n_log_m_), which is the bound we will use in the following discussions.

The significance of Recurrence (11) is that every recursive subproblem has the form _T(q,q_). In other words, after one application of the recurrence, the problem becomes symmetric. Therefore, the tools developed in the previous sections (e.g., Theorems 1 and 3) can be applied directly to _T(q,q_).

It is also useful to observe that _r_<sup>2</sup>_q_<sup>4/3</sup>=_m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>, which is precisely the complexity term appearing in Theorem 6.

## 6.2.1 The first main procedure

We begin with the following approximate counting lemma.

**Lemma 12** (Approximate Counting)**.** _For any interval I, one can compute in O(n_log_m_) _time an integer_ \(\hat{\kappa}(I)\) _satisfying_ \(|\kappa(I)-\hat{\kappa}(I)|\le c_0m^2\) _for some constant c_<sub>0</sub>_\>_0.

_Proof._ We invoke the standard subroutine and return \(\hat{\kappa}(I)=\sum_{A_t\times B_t\in\Gamma}|A_t||B_t|\). The running time is _O(n_log_m_).

Clearly, \(|\kappa(I)-\hat{\kappa}(I)|\) is bounded by the number of uncertain pairs recorded in the recursive subproblems of _T(q,q_). There are _O(r_<sup>2</sup>) such subproblems, each contributing at most _O(q_<sup>2</sup>) pairs. Hence \(|\kappa(I)-\hat{\kappa}(I)|=O(r^2q^2)=O(m^2)\), since _r=n/m_ and _q=m_<sup>2</sup>_/n_. \(\square\)

Lemma 12 immediately yields the following quasi-decision lemma, whose proof is similar to that of Theorem 2.

**Lemma 13** (Quasi-Decision)**.** _Given an interval I and an integer K with_ \(1\le K\le mn\)_, there exists an O(n_log_m)-time algorithm whose output has one of the following three outcomes: (1) the algorithm reports_ \(\kappa(I)<K\)_; (2) the algorithm reports_ \(\kappa(I)>K\)_; (3) the algorithm reports "unsure", in which case_ \(|\kappa(I)-K|\le c_0m^2\) _for some constant c_<sub>0</sub>_\>_0.

We now describe the first main procedure. Its goal is to reduce the number of candidate distances from _O(mn_) to _O(m_<sup>2</sup>) while maintaining an interval _I_ containing \(\delta^*\).

Initially, \(I=(0,+\infty)\), and therefore \(|S\cap I|=O(mn)\). The algorithm proceeds in iterations. In each iteration, which runs in _O(n_log_m_) time, the number of candidate distances is reduced by a constant factor. After _O_(log(_n/m_)) iterations, we obtain an interval _I_ containing \(\delta^*\) such that \(|S\cap I|=O(m^2)\).

Since each iteration takes _O(n_log_m_) time, the total running time of the procedure is bounded by _O(n_log_m_log(_n/m_)), which is _O(n_log<sup>2</sup>_m_) since _n\<m_<sup>2</sup>.

### A general _j_-th iteration.

Suppose we are given an interval _I_<sub>_j_-1</sub>. The goal is to compute an interval _I<sub>j</sub>_ such that either

1. \(|S\cap I_j|=O(m^2)\), in which case the first main procedure terminates; or<tbc>

2. \(|S\cap I_j|\le\rho|S\cap I_{j-1}|\) for some constant \(\rho<1\).<tbc>

We begin by invoking the standard subroutine. The running time is _O(n_log_m_). Recall that \(N(\Gamma)\) denote the number of pairs recorded by the bicliques of \(\Gamma\). Let _M_ denote the total number of uncertain pairs contained in the recursive subproblems _T(q,q_). As shown in the proof of Lemma 12, _M=O(m_<sup>2</sup>). Thus we may assume that \(M\le c_1m^2\) for some constant _c_<sub>1</sub>_\>_0.

If \(N(\Gamma)\le c_2m^2\) for a sufficiently large constant _c_<sub>2</sub>, then \(|S\cap I_{j-1}|=N(\Gamma)+M=O(m^2)\). Hence, in this case, the first main procedure terminates and returns _I_<sub>_j_-1</sub>. Assume therefore that \(N(\Gamma)>c_2m^2\).

We next construct the expander graphs for the bicliques of \(\Gamma\) and form a weighted distance set _E_ exactly as in Section 5.1. Since the total size of the bicliques in \(\Gamma\) is _O(n_log_m_), this step takes _O(n_log_m_) time. We then partition _E_ into _O_(1) basic intervals and use Lemma 13 in place of the quasi-decision algorithm from Section 5.1. This yields an interval _I<sub>j</sub>_.

Using analysis similar to Section 5.2, we can prove \(|S\cap I_j|\le\rho\cdot|S\cap I_{j-1}|\) for some constant \(\rho<1\). Intuitively, we can make _c_<sub>2</sub> large enough so that _M_ and the term _c_<sub>0</sub>_m_<sup>2</sup> in Lemma 13 can be neglected compared to _c_<sub>2</sub>_m_<sup>2</sup>. For example, if we follow the same notation as in Section 5.2, then we have _m_<sub>_j_-1</sub>=_N(T_) and \(m'_{j-1}\le M\). Since \(M\le c_1m^2\) and \(N(\Gamma)>c_2m^2\), we have \(m'_{j-1}\le\frac{c_1}{c_2}\cdot m_{j-1}\). Since \(n_{j-1}=m_{j-1}+m'_{j-1}\), it follows that \(m'_{j-1}\le\frac{c_1}{c_1+c_2}\cdot n_{j-1}\). This inequality can be used to replace \(m'_{j-1}\le 0.6n_{j-1}\) that was obtained by Theorem 3 (note that here \(\Gamma\) plays the role of Theorem 3 and that is why we do not have an explicit distance representation theorem here). Similarly, we can prove \(|S\cap\hat{I}|\le 2c_0m^2\) as a counterpart to Lemma 9.

Therefore, each iteration runs in _O(n_log_m_) time and reduces the number of candidate distances by a constant factor. After _O_(log(_n/m_)) iterations, we obtain an interval _I_ containing \(\delta^*\) such that \(|S\cap I|=O(m^2)\). The total running time of the first main procedure is _O(n_log<sup>2</sup>_m_).

## 6.2.2 The second main procedure

We now describe the second main procedure, which is the most challenging part of the asymmetric distance selection algorithm.

Given an interval _I_ containing \(\delta^*\) with \(|S\cap I|=O(m^2)\), the goal is to shrink _I_ so that \(|S\cap I|=O(m^{2/3}n^{2/3})\) while maintaining \(\delta^*\in I\).

We begin with the following approximate counting lemma.

**Lemma 14** (Approximate Counting)**.** _Let I be an interval. For every integer i with_ \(1\le i\le O(\mathrm{log}^*q)\)_, one can compute an integer_ \(\hat{\kappa}(I)\) _such that_

\(|\kappa(I)-\hat{\kappa}(I)|\le c_0^*m^{2/3}n^{2/3}(\mathrm{log}^{(i)}q)^4\)

_for some constant_ \(c_0^*>0\)_. The running time is O(n_log_m+m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>/log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_q_) _for i_=1,2_, and O(n_log_m+m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>/(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_q_)<sup>2</sup>) _for_ \(i\ge 3\).

_Proof._ We only discuss the case \(i\ge 3\); the cases _i_=1,2 are analogous.

We first invoke the standard subroutine in _O(n_log_m_) time and add the number of pairs recorded by the resulting bicliques \(\Gamma\) to \(\hat{\kappa}(I)\).

For each recursive subproblem _T(q,q_) in Recurrence (11), it is for a subset \(A'\subseteq A\) and \(B'\subseteq B\) with \(|A'|\le q\) and \(|B'|\le q\). Let \(\kappa'(I)\) denote the number of distances between \(A'\) and \(B'\) lying in _I_. Apply Theorem 1 to \((A',B')\) with _i_ and _I_ yields a number \(\hat{\kappa}'(I)\) that approximates \(\kappa'(I)\) with error bounded by _c_<sub>0</sub>_q_<sup>4/3</sup>(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_q_)<sup>4</sup>. The runtime is _O(q_<sup>4/3</sup>/(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_q_)<sup>2</sup>). We add \(\hat{\kappa}'(I)\) to \(\hat{\kappa}(I)\).

Since there are _O(r_<sup>2</sup>) subproblems, the total error is bounded by

\(O(r^2)\cdot c_0q^{4/3}(\mathrm{log}^{(i)}q)^4=O(m^{2/3}n^{2/3}(\mathrm{log}^{(i)}q)^4),\)

where we use the identity _r_<sup>2</sup>_q_<sup>4/3</sup>=_m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>.

Similarly, the total time spent on all subproblems is

\(O(r^2)\cdot O\left(\frac{q^{4/3}}{(log^{(i)}q)^2}\right)=O\left(\frac{m^{2/3}n^{2/3}}{(log^{(i)}q)^2}\right).\)

Adding the _O(n_log_m_) time of the standard subroutine completes the proof.

Lemma 14 immediately yields the following quasi-decision lemma, whose proof is similar to that of Theorem 2.

**Lemma 15** (Quasi-Decision)**.** _Given an interval I and an integer K with_ \(1\le K\le mn\)_, for every i with_ \(1\le i\le O(log^*q)\)_, there exists an algorithm whose output has one of the following three outcomes: (1) the algorithm reports_ \(\kappa(I)<K\)_; (2) the algorithm reports_ \(\kappa(I)>K\)_; (3) the algorithm reports "unsure", in which case_ \(|\kappa(I)-K|\le c_0^*m^{2/3}n^{2/3}(log^{(i)}q)^4\) _for some constant_ \(c_0^*>0\)_. The running time is O(n_log_m+m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>/log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_q_) _for i_=1,2_, and O(n_log_m+m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>/log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_q_)<sup>2</sup>) _for_ \(i\ge 3\).

We now describe the second main procedure. The framework is identical to that of Section 5.

Recall that \(|S\cap I|=O(m^2)\) and \(\delta^*\in I\). The algorithm proceeds in phases. For _i_=1,2_,...,O_(log<sup>∗</sup>_q_), the goal of the _i_-th phase is to transform an interval _I_ satisfying<tbc>

\(|S\cap I|=O(m^{2/3}n^{2/3}(log^{(i-1)}q)^4)\)

<tbc>(and _O(m_<sup>2</sup>) when _i_=1) into a smaller interval \(I'\subseteq I\) satisfying

\(|S\cap I'|=O(m^{2/3}n^{2/3}(log^{(i)}q)^4)\)

while maintaining \(\delta^*\in I'\).

Initially, \(|S\cap I|=O(m^2)\). After _O_(log<sup>∗</sup>_q_) phases, we obtain an interval _I_ satisfying \(|S\cap I|=O(m^{2/3}n^{2/3})\), which is precisely the goal of the second main procedure. Each phase consists of _O_(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_q_) iterations. Each iteration runs in _O(n_log_m+m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>/log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_q_) time for _i_=1,2, and in _O(n_log_m+m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>/(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_q_)<sup>2</sup>) time for \(i\ge 3\). Consequently, the total running time over all phases is<tbc>

\(O(nlogm)\cdot\sum_{i=1}^{O(log^*q)}log^{(i)}q+O(m^{2/3}n^{2/3})\cdot\left(1+\sum_{i=3}^{O(log^*q)}\frac{1}{log^{(i)}q}\right),\)

<tbc>which is

\(O(nlogmlogq)+O(m^{2/3}n^{2/3})=O(nlog^2m+m^{2/3}n^{2/3}),\)

since \(q=m^2/n\le m\).

## Algorithm description.

We describe a general _i_-th phase. Before the phase begins, we are given an interval _I_ satisfying \(|S\cap I|=O(m^{2/3}n^{2/3}(log^{(i-1)}q)^4)\) and containing \(\delta^*\). The goal is to compute a subinterval \(I'\subseteq I\) such that \(|S\cap I'|=O(m^{2/3}n^{2/3}(log^{(i)}q)^4)\) and \(\delta^*\in I'\).

As in Section 5, the phase proceeds in iterations. At the beginning of the _j_-th iteration, we are given an interval _I_<sub>_j_-1</sub> containing \(\delta^*\), with _I_<sub>0</sub>=_I_. Each iteration either

1. produces a smaller interval \(I_j\subseteq I_{j-1}\) such that \(\delta^*\in I_j\) and \(|S\cap I_j|\le\rho|S\cap I_{j-1}|\) for some constant \(\rho<1\); or<tbc>

2. produces a smaller interval \(I_j\subseteq I_{j-1}\) such that \(\delta^*\in I_j\) and \(|S\cap I_j|\le c^*m^{2/3}n^{2/3}(log^{(i)}q)^4\) for a sufficiently large constant _c_<sup>∗</sup>.<tbc>

Since the phase starts with \(|S\cap I|=O(m^{2/3}n^{2/3}(\mathrm{log}^{(i-1)}q)^4)\), the first outcome can occur only _O_(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_q_) times before the second outcome must occur.<sup>2</sup> Unlike the symmetric case algorithm, we do not have an efficient test for whether the second outcome has already occurred. Instead, we simply run the phase for \(\hat{c}\mathrm{log}^{(i)}q\) iterations, where \(\hat{c}\) is a sufficiently large constant depending on \(\rho\) and _c_<sup>∗</sup>.

In the following, we describe a single iteration. For simplicity, we assume \(i\ge 3\). The cases _i_=1,2 are identical except for the running-time bounds. We assume that

\(|S\cap I_{j-1}|\ge c^*m^{2/3}n^{2/3}(\mathrm{log}^{(i)}q)^4,\)

since otherwise the second outcome already holds.

We first invoke the standard subroutine in _O(n_log_m_) time, obtaining a collection \(\Gamma\) of bicliques. We use index _p_ to refer to a recursive subproblem _T(q,q_) in Recurrence (11). For each subproblem _p_, it is associated with a subset \(A_p\subseteq A\) and \(B_p\subseteq B\) with \(|A_p|\le q\) and \(|B_p|\le q\). Let _S<sub>p</sub>_ denote the set of interpoint distances between _A<sub>p</sub>_ and _B<sub>p</sub>_. Depending on the context, _S<sub>p</sub>_ may also refer to the corresponding point pairs.

Let _S_<sub>0</sub> denote the set of distances of _S_ that are not in _S<sub>p</sub>_ for any subproblem _p_. Then _S_<sub>0</sub> and the sets _S<sub>p</sub>_ for all subproblems _p_ form a partition of _S_. Moreover, \(S_0\cap I_{j-1}\) is precisely the set of distances recorded by \(\Gamma\).

For every subproblem _p_, we apply Theorem 3 to (_A<sub>p</sub>,B<sub>p</sub>_) and _I_<sub>_j_-1</sub> with parameter _i_. This produces a collection of bicliques \(\Gamma_p\) in _O(q_<sup>4/3</sup>/(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_q_)<sup>2</sup>) time. Since there are _O(r_<sup>2</sup>) subproblems, the total running time is \(O(r^2)\cdot O(q^{4/3}/(\mathrm{log}^{(i)}q)^2)=O(m^{2/3}n^{2/3}/(\mathrm{log}^{(i)}q)^2)\).

Let \(N(\Gamma_p)\) denote the number of pairs recorded by \(\Gamma_p\).

We call a subproblem _p bounded_ if \(N(\Gamma_p)\le c_1q^{4/3}(\mathrm{log}^{(i)}q)^4\), where _c_<sub>1</sub> is the constant from Theorem 3; otherwise _p_ is _unbounded_. Let _P_<sub>1</sub> and _P_<sub>2</sub> denote the sets of bounded and unbounded subproblems, respectively. Define \(S_1=\bigcup_{p\in P_1}S_p\), \(S_2=\bigcup_{p\in P_2}S_p\), and \(S_{02}=S_0\cup S_2\). Then _S_<sub>02</sub> and _S_<sub>1</sub> form a partition of _S_.

For every bounded subproblem \(p\in P_1\), Lemma 6 implies that \(|S_p\cap I_{j-1}|=O(q^{4/3}(\mathrm{log}^{(i)}q)^4)\). Since there are _O(r_<sup>2</sup>) bounded subproblems, \(|S_1\cap I_{j-1}|=O(m^{2/3}n^{2/3}(\mathrm{log}^{(i)}q)^4)\). Hence, for some constant \(c'>0\),<tbc>

\(|S_1\cap I_{j-1}|\le c'm^{2/3}n^{2/3}(\mathrm{log}^{(i)}q)^4.\)

<tbc>Combining this with the assumption on \(|S\cap I_{j-1}|\) yields

\(|S_1\cap I_{j-1}|\le\frac{c'}{c^*}|S\cap I_{j-1}|.\) (12)

Observe that _S_<sub>1</sub> plays exactly the role of the distances of the unresolved pairs in the symmetric analysis.

For the bicliques in \(\Gamma\) and in all collections \(\Gamma_p\) with \(p\in P_2\), we construct expander graphs and form a weighted distance set _E_ exactly as in Section 5.1. The total size of the bicliques in \(\Gamma\) is _O(n_log_m_), while the total size of all bicliques in \(\Gamma_p\) over all \(p\in P_2\) is \(O(r^2)\cdot O(q^{4/3}/(\mathrm{log}^{(i)}q)^2)=O(m^{2/3}n^{2/3}/(\mathrm{log}^{(i)}q)^2)\). Hence, constructing all expander graphs and the set _E_ takes _O(n_log_m+m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>/(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_q_)<sup>2</sup>) time.

Finally, we test the values of _E_ exactly as in Section 5.1, using Lemma 15 in place of Theorem 2. This yields an interval _I<sub>j</sub>_.

Since only _O_(1) quasi-decision calls are required, the total running time of the iteration remains _O(n_log_m+m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>/(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_q_)<sup>2</sup>).

<sup>2</sup>Note that for _i_=1, the number of candidate distances decreases from _O(m_<sup>2</sup>) to _O(m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>(log_q_)<sup>4</sup>). Since _m_<sup>2</sup>/(_m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>(log_q_)<sup>4</sup>)=_q_<sup>2/3</sup>/(log_q_)<sup>4</sup>, this requires only _O_(log_q_) iterations.

### Algorithm Correctness.

Using an argument analogous to the proof of Lemma 7, one can show that

\(|S_{02}\cap I_j|\le\rho'|S_{02}\cap I_{j-1}|\) (13)

for some constant \(\rho'<1\). The only additional ingredient is that, for every unbounded subproblem \(p\in P_2\), by definition, \(N(\Gamma_p)>c_1q^{4/3}(\mathrm{log}^{(i)}q)^4\). Since \(|S_p\cap I_{j-1}|\ge N(\Gamma_p)\), we have \(|S_p\cap I_{j-1}|>c_1q^{4/3}(\mathrm{log}^{(i)}q)^4\). Consequently, \(N(\Gamma_p)\ge 0.4|S_p\cap I_{j-1}|\) by Theorem 3.

We now prove that

\(|S\cap I_j|\le\rho|S\cap I_{j-1}|\)

for some constant \(\rho<1\).

Since _S_<sub>02</sub> and _S_<sub>1</sub> form a partition of _S_,<tbc>

\(|S\cap I_j|=|S_1\cap I_j|+|S_{02}\cap I_j|.\)

<tbc>Because \(I_j\subseteq I_{j-1}\), we have \(S_1\cap I_j\subseteq S_1\cap I_{j-1}\). Therefore,<tbc>

\(|S\cap I_j|\le|S_1\cap I_{j-1}|+|S_{02}\cap I_j|.\)

<tbc>Combining (12) and (13) yields

\(|S\cap I_j|\le\frac{c'}{c^*}|S\cap I_{j-1}|+\rho'|S_{02}\cap I_{j-1}|\le\left(\frac{c'}{c^*}+\rho'\right)|S\cap I_{j-1}|.\)

Since \(\rho'<1\), choosing _c_<sup>∗</sup> sufficiently large and defining \(\rho=\frac{c'}{c^*}+\rho'\) gives \(\rho<1\). This proves the first outcome of the iteration.

The above analysis assumes that \(|S\cap I_{j-1}|\ge c^*m^{2/3}n^{2/3}(\mathrm{log}^{(i)}q)^4\). Otherwise, we simply run the same algorithm, which obtains an interval \(I_j\subseteq I_{j-1}\) containing \(\delta^*\). Since \(|S\cap I_j|\le|S\cap I_{j-1}|\le c^*m^{2/3}n^{2/3}(\mathrm{log}^{(i)}q)^4\), the second outcome holds automatically.

Therefore, in each iteration, we simply run the same algorithm as above. Every iteration either reduces the number of candidate distances by a constant factor or reaches the target bound _O(m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>(log<sup>(_i_)</sup>_q_)<sup>4</sup>).

### Summary.

We conclude that, within _O(n_log<sup>2</sup>_m+m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>) time, we can compute an interval _I_ containing \(\delta^*\) such that \(|S\cap I|=O(m^{2/3}n^{2/3})\).

## 6.2.3 The distance-reporting procedure

We are given an interval _I_ containing \(\delta^*\) such that \(|S\cap I|=O(m^{2/3}n^{2/3})\). The goal of this procedure is to compute \(\delta^*\).

Assume that \(I=(\alpha,\beta]\). We first compute \(K_\alpha\), the number of distances in _S_ that are at most \(\alpha\). This can be done in _O(m_log_n+n_log_m+m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>) time \[24\]. Consequently, \(\delta^*\) is the \((K-K_\alpha)\)-th smallest distance in \(S\cap I\). Thus it suffices to enumerate all distances in \(S\cap I\) and then apply the linear-time selection algorithm. The latter step takes _O(m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>) time since \(|S\cap I|=O(m^{2/3}n^{2/3})\).

The remaining task is therefore to enumerate all distances in \(S\cap I\). For this, we have the following more general result.

**Lemma 16.** _Given any interval I, all distances in_ \(S\cap I\) _can be enumerated in_ \(O(n\mathrm{log}m+m^{2/3}n^{2/3}+|S\cap I|)\) _time._

_Proof._ We first invoke the standard subroutine in _O(n_log_m_) time, obtaining a collection \(\Gamma\) of bicliques. All distances recorded by \(\Gamma\) are then reported explicitly, requiring constant time per output distance.

For each recursive subproblem _T(q,q_) in Recurrence (11), it is associated with a subset \(A'\subseteq A\) and \(B'\subseteq B\) with \(|A'|\le q\) and \(|B'|\le q\). By Corollary 2, all distances between \(A'\) and \(B'\) lying in _I_ can be enumerated in _O(q_<sup>4/3</sup>) time, in addition to constant time per output distance. Since there are _O(r_<sup>2</sup>) subproblems, the total time spent on all subproblems is _O(r_<sup>2</sup>_q_<sup>4/3</sup>)=_O(m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>), again in addition to constant time per output distance.

Combining the contributions of \(\Gamma\) and all recursive subproblems proves the lemma.

Applying the above lemma and using the bound \(|S\cap I|=O(m^{2/3}n^{2/3})\), all distances in \(S\cap I\) can be enumerated in _O(n_log_m+m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>) time. A final linear-time selection then computes \(\delta^*\) within the same asymptotic bound.

### 6.2.4 Wrapping things up

We have shown that, for the case _n\<m_<sup>2</sup>, the first main procedure requires _O(n_log<sup>2</sup>_m_) time, the second main procedure requires _O(n_log<sup>2</sup>_m+m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>) time, and the distance-reporting procedure requires _O(n_log_m+m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>) time. Therefore, the overall running time is _O(n_log<sup>2</sup>_m+m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>). This establishes Theorem 6 for the case \(m\le n<m^2\).

Combining this with the case \(n\ge m^2\), we conclude that if \(m\le n\), then the distance selection problem can be solved in _O(n_log<sup>2</sup>_m+m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>) time.

If _m\>n_, the roles of _A_ and _B_ can be exchanged, yielding a running time of _O(m_log<sup>2</sup>_n+m_<sup>2/3</sup>_n_<sup>2/3</sup>).

Combining the two bounds proves Theorem 6.
